title: Memory flows: geometry and dynamics of sequential retrieval in input-driven Hopfield networks
summary: Associative memory models classically describe retrieval as convergence to stored patterns, but the theory of sequential retrieval remains comparatively limited. We develop a two-timescale input-driven Hopfield network in which fast associative retrieval is modulated by a slow feedback variable evolving over a prescribed memory-transition graph. This yields autonomous, graph-constrained transitions while preserving analytical tractability. Using slow-fast and geometric singular perturbation theory, we characterize memory fixation via memory manifolds and identify the geometric regions that govern stability loss and escape from retrieved memories. We further derive reduced slow dynamics and explicit criteria for transition onset, self-sustained retrieval, and collapse, expressed through escape times, gain thresholds, and fixed points. Together, these results provide a tractable framework for analyzing feedback-driven sequential retrieval in Hopfield networks.

AI.tldr: A two-timescale input-driven Hopfield network models sequential memory retrieval as autonomous, graph-constrained transitions, analyzed via slow-fast and geometric singular perturbation theory.
AI.motivation: Classical associative memory theory explains retrieval as convergence to stored patterns, but a rigorous account of sequential retrieval remains comparatively underdeveloped, motivating a tractable model of ordered memory transitions.
AI.method: The authors construct a two-timescale input-driven Hopfield network where fast associative retrieval is modulated by a slow feedback variable evolving over a prescribed memory-transition graph. Using slow-fast and geometric singular perturbation theory, they characterize memory fixation via memory manifolds and identify geometric regions governing stability loss and escape; they derive reduced slow dynamics and explicit criteria for transition onset, self-sustained retrieval, and collapse.
AI.result: The analysis yields reduced slow dynamics and explicit conditions—expressed through escape times, gain thresholds, and fixed points—that delineate transition onset, self-sustained sequential retrieval, and collapse, with stability-loss and escape regions characterized geometrically.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an analytically tractable account of feedback-driven sequential retrieval in Hopfield networks, linking fast attractor dynamics to slow graph-constrained control and offering testable criteria for reliable sequences.

title: How Path Integral Diffusion Decides a Finite Spin Glass
summary: When an AI diffusion-type generator samples a frustrated spin glass, which macroscopic alternatives does it decide first, and when? We study this for bridge-diffusion models of the Path Integral Diffusion (PID) type started from a point source. We show that every isotropic PID is a time-changed Gaussian stochastic localization, and conversely every signal-to-noise schedule is realized by a PID protocol. What a continuous-time generator decides therefore does not depend on the protocol, which only sets when and at what cost. We describe the generator's state by its partial commitments: the probabilities it assigns, at each moment, to nested classes of configurations fixed by the target. The partial commitments are martingales that move only along class contrasts. Their ensemble average gives the information about each level at an exact rate set by squared magnetization contrasts. Each split is decided, approximately, like a binary Gaussian channel at signal-to-noise ratio 1.04/λ_P, with λ_P the leading eigenvalue of the parent's correlation matrix. The theory is applied to Bethe-lattice and Sherrington--Kirkpatrick (SK) glasses with up to 64 spins. It is observed generically that a trajectory first shifts its weight to one of the two mirror halves of the zero-field measure and then to the glassy classes inside it. These classes appear near the glass transition and keep their identity on cooling. Nested glassy levels have similar λ_P and are decided together, so a trajectory commits in one or two distinct events---the mirror choice and a compound glassy decision---which separate further with coupling and size, as the spectra predict. For a generator that takes finitely many steps, the protocol matters through the late, local stage rather than the macroscopic decisions.

AI.tldr: Isotropic Path Integral Diffusion generators of spin glasses are equivalent to time-changed Gaussian stochastic localization, so the sequence of macroscopic decisions is protocol-independent. Partial-commitment martingales predict that trajectories commit in one or two events: a mirror (Z2) choice then a compound glassy decision.
AI.motivation: To understand which macroscopic alternatives an AI diffusion-type generator samples first and when, when denoising a frustrated spin glass, and to disentangle what is intrinsic to the continuous-time generator from what is set by the diffusion protocol.
AI.method: Study bridge-diffusion models of Path Integral Diffusion type started from a point source. Prove an equivalence between isotropic PID and time-changed Gaussian stochastic localization (and conversely realize every SNR schedule by a PID protocol). Describe the generator state by partial commitments—probabilities assigned to nested target-fixed configuration classes—which are martingales moving only along class contrasts; their ensemble average yields per-level information at rates set by squared magnetization contrasts, with splits behaving approximately as binary Gaussian channels at SNR 1.04/λ_P, where λ_P is the leading eigenvalue of the parent correlation matrix. Apply to Bethe-lattice and Sherrington–Kirkpatrick glasses up to 64 spins.
AI.result: Partial commitments are martingales driven only by class contrasts, with information accumulation at rates proportional to squared magnetization contrasts, and each split acts approximately as a Gaussian channel at SNR 1.04/λ_P. Empirically, trajectories generically first shift weight to one of the two mirror halves of the zero-field measure, then to glassy classes inside it; glassy classes emerge near the glass transition and retain identity on cooling. Nested glassy levels share similar λ_P and are decided together, giving one or two commitment events (mirror choice plus compound glassy decision), which separate further with coupling and system size as spectra predict.
AI.conclusion: What a continuous-time generator decides is protocol-independent; the protocol only fixes when and at what cost. Macroscopic decisions are one or two events (mirror, then compound glassy), and for finitely stepped generators protocol effects appear in the late, local stage rather than in the macroscopic decisions.

title: Spatial effects of Kuramoto modeling on the power-grid frequencies
summary:
Spatial coupling and heterogeneity can generate complex power-grid frequency dynamics. We investigate the contributions of spatial structure, intrinsic nonlinear dynamics, and external driving using the Kuramoto model (KM), with and without uncorrelated noise, and compare its predictions with real-grid measurements.
  We analyse one month of 100 ms frequency measurements from 16 Hungarian transmission-grid sites and simulate the KM on a 387-node transmission network and two-dimensional lattices. The measured power spectra exhibit two scaling regimes, with exponents of approximately 1.63 and 2.23. One-second frequency increments decorrelate rapidly, while correlations of their local inverse variance decay slowly, initially as a power law, $τ^{-0.26(2)}$, up to 15 minutes. A superstatistical Gaussian mixture based on measured local variances captures much of the non-Gaussian increment distribution, but not the rare extreme events.
  We also estimate the non-stationary long-time frequency autocorrelation exponent. KM simulations on low-dimensional networks exhibit algebraically decaying autocorrelations and power spectra, consistent with the measurements and the Wiener-Khinchin relation in the steady state. On the heterogeneous transmission network, partial synchronization and frequency locking produce persistent spatial patterns and multi-peaked frequency distributions. However, neither deterministic KM dynamics nor independent Gaussian driving reproduces the measured spectra and increment statistics simultaneously. Moreover, empirical frequency fluctuations are largely shared across substations, whereas simulated fluctuations mainly reflect relative node motion. These findings suggest that spatially coupled nonlinear dynamics contribute to observed frequency fluctuations alongside external driving, including 15-minute power dispatches.

AI.tldr: Analysis of one month of 100 ms frequency data from 16 Hungarian grid sites, combined with Kuramoto-model simulations on a 387-node transmission network and 2D lattices, shows that spatially coupled nonlinear dynamics and external driving jointly shape power-grid frequency fluctuations, though neither alone reproduces all measured statistics.
AI.motivation: Spatial coupling and heterogeneity are known to generate complex power-grid frequency dynamics, but the relative roles of spatial structure, intrinsic nonlinear dynamics, and external driving in producing observed frequency statistics remain unclear and are rarely tested against real-grid measurements.
AI.method: Frequency measurements at 100 ms resolution over one month from 16 Hungarian transmission-grid sites were analyzed (power spectra, 1 s frequency increments, local inverse-variance correlations, superstatistical Gaussian-mixture modeling). Simulations used the Kuramoto model, with and without uncorrelated noise, on a 387-node transmission network and on two-dimensional lattices; the non-stationary long-time frequency autocorrelation exponent was also estimated and compared with the Wiener-Khinchin relation.
AI.result: Measured power spectra show two scaling regimes with exponents ≈1.63 and ≈2.23. One-second frequency increments decorrelate rapidly, while correlations of their local inverse variance decay slowly, initially as τ^(-0.26(2)) up to 15 minutes. A superstatistical Gaussian mixture based on measured local variances captures much of the non-Gaussian increment distribution but not rare extreme events. KM on low-dimensional networks yields algebraically decaying autocorrelations and power spectra consistent with measurements. On the heterogeneous transmission network, partial synchronization and frequency locking produce persistent spatial patterns and multi-peaked frequency distributions. However, neither deterministic KM dynamics nor independent Gaussian driving simultaneously reproduces the measured spectra and increment statistics; empirical fluctuations are largely shared across substations, whereas simulated fluctuations mainly reflect relative node motion.
AI.conclusion: Spatially coupled nonlinear dynamics contribute to observed grid frequency fluctuations alongside external driving, including 15-minute power dispatches; single-mechanism models (deterministic KM or independent Gaussian driving) are insufficient, motivating models that combine intrinsic nonlinear spatial dynamics with external forcing.

title: Entanglement percolation enhanced by the power of choice
summary: Quantum communication networks are best supported by maximally entangled states, but imperfections in entanglement generation and distribution generally limit the distributed states to being only partially entangled. Therefore, protocols typically consisting of local operations and classical communication are required to create suitably entangled networks. Here, we introduce a power-of-choice (PoC) protocol based on reversing the selection criteria in the Achlioptas process previously considered in classical explosive percolation. The resulting PoC protocol anticipates the entanglement percolation transition, thereby reducing the entanglement resources needed to establish quantum communication. Notably, in contrast to explosive percolation, the PoC protocol admits an implementation using local information with no appreciable loss of performance.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a power-of-choice (PoC) protocol that anticipates the entanglement percolation transition to reduce entanglement resources for quantum networks, and show it can be implemented locally.
AI.motivation: Quantum communication networks require maximally entangled states, but generation and distribution imperfections yield only partially entangled states; local operations and classical communication (LOCC) protocols are needed to build suitable entangled networks. Reducing the entanglement resources required for a percolation transition is therefore desirable.
AI.method: A power-of-choice (PoC) protocol derived by reversing the selection criteria of the Achlioptas process used in classical explosive percolation. The protocol anticipates (moves forward) the entanglement percolation transition. The authors also examine implementation feasibility using only local information.
AI.result: The PoC protocol anticipates the entanglement percolation transition, reducing the entanglement resources needed to establish quantum communication. Unlike explosive percolation, it admits a local-information implementation with no appreciable loss of performance.
AI.conclusion: A resource-efficient, locally implementable protocol for entanglement percolation is achieved, offering a practical route to quantum communication networks with reduced entanglement demands.

title: Regev's Reduction Reaches Reconstruction
summary: Regev's reduction uses a quantum Fourier transform to carry out reductions between various problems related to lattices and codes. We apply it to the problem of sampling from Gibbs distributions of certain classical spin glass Hamiltonians, which can equivalently be thought of as cost functions for average-case instances of an optimization problem called $D$-regular max-$k$-LINSAT. This problem becomes hard at low temperature. Here, we use a quantum decoding algorithm called Belief Propagation with Quantum Messages (BPQM) to solve the decoding problem arising from Regev's reduction. Our main contribution is a proof that the minimum temperature reachable using Regev+BPQM is exactly equal to the reconstruction threshold temperature for noisy channels transmitting signals on a tree network. This equality can be understood via Renes' duality between classical and quantum channels, which we use to show that quantum decoding is possible exactly when classical reconstruction on the dual problem is impossible. M{é}zard and Montanari identified this reconstruction temperature with a dynamical glass transition predicted by the one-step replica-symmetry breaking (1RSB) cavity equation. It is conjectured that local samplers such as Metropolis Monte Carlo and Glauber dynamics cannot equilibrate efficiently below this reconstruction temperature but may do so above it; our large numerical experiments show close agreement with this prediction across hundreds of different problem parameters. Therefore, our results rigorously show that Regev+BPQM reaches a temperature for which, to our knowledge, there is no matching classical guarantee, and brings Regev+BPQM to the conjectured limit of efficient Gibbs sampling by classical local dynamics.

AI.tldr: Regev's reduction combined with the BPQM quantum decoder samples Gibbs distributions of D-regular max-k-LINSAT at a minimum temperature exactly equal to the reconstruction threshold, which corresponds to the 1RSB dynamical glass transition and marks the conjectured limit of efficient classical local sampling.
AI.motivation: Sampling Gibbs distributions of spin-glass Hamiltonians (equivalently low-temperature average-case D-regular max-k-LINSAT) becomes hard at low temperature, and classical local samplers are conjectured to fail below the reconstruction threshold set by the 1RSB dynamical glass transition. The paper seeks a rigorous quantum method that reaches this limit.
AI.method: The authors apply Regev's reduction (based on the quantum Fourier transform) to the Gibbs sampling problem, and solve the resulting decoding problem with Belief Propagation with Quantum Messages (BPQM). They prove the minimum reachable temperature equals the reconstruction threshold for noisy tree channels, using Renes' classical-quantum channel duality to link quantum decoding success to impossibility of classical reconstruction on the dual problem. Large numerical experiments compare against classical local dynamics predictions.
AI.result: The authors prove that the minimum temperature reachable by Regev+BPQM is exactly the reconstruction threshold temperature, and via Renes' duality show quantum decoding succeeds exactly when classical reconstruction on the dual problem fails. Experiments across hundreds of parameter settings show close agreement with the predicted 1RSB dynamical glass transition.
AI.conclusion: Regev+BPQM rigorously reaches a temperature for which no matching classical guarantee is known, attaining the conjectured limit of efficient Gibbs sampling by classical local dynamics (Metropolis Monte Carlo, Glauber dynamics).

title: Bayes-Optimal Quantum Computational Sensing via Convex Spectral Design
summary: Quantum computational sensing performs task-specific inference directly through coherent sensing dynamics, avoiding an intermediate estimation step. Existing designs, however, typically optimize quantum control parameters through nonconvex programs whose performance can depend strongly on initialization. This contribution formulates binary phase classification directly in terms of the sensor's measurement response. For a fixed query budget, generalized quantum signal processing (GQSP) restricts this response to a bounded trigonometric polynomial, while the Bayes classification error is linear in the response. These properties yield an exact finite-dimensional semidefinite program for the globally Bayes-optimal sensor response. Fejér--Riesz factorization and GQSP synthesis then recover a physically realizable control sequence. The same formulation extends naturally to sample-based design and additive phase uncertainty. Numerical tests show improved accuracy and optimization reliability over direct control-angle training; noise-aware redesign also lowers error under phase uncertainty.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates binary phase classification in quantum computational sensing as an exact finite-dimensional semidefinite program by expressing the sensor's measurement response via generalized quantum signal processing (GQSP), yielding globally Bayes-optimal control sequences.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum computational sensing designs optimize control parameters through nonconvex programs whose performance depends strongly on initialization. The authors seek a globally optimal, initialization-independent design for binary phase classification.
AI.method: Binary phase classification is posed directly in terms of the sensor's measurement response. For a fixed query budget, GQSP constrains the response to a bounded trigonometric polynomial, and the Bayes classification error is linear in the response. These properties yield an exact finite-dimensional SDP for the globally Bayes-optimal response; Fejér--Riesz factorization and GQSP synthesis then recover a physically realizable control sequence. The formulation extends to sample-based design and additive phase uncertainty.
AI.result: Numerical tests show improved accuracy and optimization reliability compared with direct control-angle training; noise-aware redesign further lowers error under phase uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Casting computational-sensing design as a convex SDP over GQSP-constrained responses enables globally optimal, reliable control synthesis, and naturally accommodates sampling and phase noise.

title: Symplectic Reck: In-Situ Learning of Gaussian Quantum Operations
summary: Programmable photonic circuits are a natural platform for physical learning, where hardware parameters are trained directly from measured feedback. We propose a physical learning algorithm and architecture for continuous-variable quantum systems where a photonic circuit is trained in situ to invert an unknown lossless Gaussian quantum operation. We prove that a generic symplectic matrix $S\in\mathrm{Sp}(2N,\mathbb{R})$ admits a decomposition into a triangular array of two-mode symplectic gates on neighboring modes, followed by single-mode symplectic gates. We then introduce the symplectic Reck mesh, which physically realizes this factorization, generalizing the unitary Reck mesh widely used in optical neural networks. When placed after an unknown Gaussian unitary, the mesh is trained in situ by nulling local response blocks one at a time using optical probes and measurements. We identify a local condition number that quantifies the squeezing required for a nulling step and its sensitivity to measurement error. We numerically demonstrate finite-shot training and robustness to systematic gate-calibration errors. Our work extends self-configuring optical networks from unitary to symplectic transformations, bringing physical learning to continuous-variable quantum photonic hardware.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a physical learning algorithm and architecture ("symplectic Reck mesh") that trains a photonic circuit in situ to invert an unknown lossless Gaussian quantum operation, extending self-configuring optical networks from unitary to symplectic transformations.
AI.motivation: Programmable photonic circuits are a natural platform for physical learning, but existing self-configuring/optical neural network meshes are built on the unitary Reck decomposition. Extending physical learning to continuous-variable quantum systems requires handling generic symplectic (Gaussian) operations, which unitary meshes cannot realize.
AI.method: The authors prove that any generic symplectic matrix S in Sp(2N,R) decomposes into a triangular array of two-mode symplectic gates on neighboring modes followed by single-mode symplectic gates. They physically realize this factorization as a "symplectic Reck mesh," generalizing the unitary Reck mesh. Placed after an unknown Gaussian unitary, the mesh is trained in situ by nulling local response blocks one at a time using optical probes and measurements. A local condition number is introduced to quantify the squeezing required per nulling step and its sensitivity to measurement error.
AI.result: The decomposition theorem for generic symplectic matrices is established. A local condition number characterizes squeezing requirements and error sensitivity of each nulling step. Numerical experiments demonstrate finite-shot training and robustness to systematic gate-calibration errors.
AI.conclusion: The work extends self-configuring optical networks from unitary to symplectic transformations, bringing physical learning to continuous-variable quantum photonic hardware and enabling in-situ inversion of unknown lossless Gaussian quantum operations.

title: Can One Hear the Size of a Clock?
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures; Supplemental Material (12 pages) included
summary: Weyl's law counts the vibration modes that fit into a cavity, and a quantum system with $d$ levels can oscillate at up to $d(d-1)/2$ frequencies without decay. For systems that jump at random between states, no such count was known: they oscillate only out of equilibrium, and the random timing of their jumps damps every oscillation. We find the missing count: if $Q$ is the ratio of frequency to decay rate, a system of $d$ states sustains fewer than $2(d-1)/(πQ)$ oscillations whose ratio exceeds $Q$. Nested cycles approach this bound, and measured oscillations reveal how large a hidden system must be.

AI.tldr: A Weyl-law analogue for classical Markov jump systems: a d-state system supports fewer than 2(d-1)/(πQ) non-equilibrium oscillations whose frequency-to-decay ratio exceeds Q, with nested cycles approaching this bound.
AI.motivation: Weyl's law counts vibration modes in a cavity, and quantum d-level systems can oscillate at up to d(d-1)/2 undamped frequencies. For systems that jump randomly between states, no analogous count existed: such systems oscillate only out of equilibrium, and stochastic jump timing damps every oscillation. The paper seeks the missing counting law for this damped, non-equilibrium setting.
AI.method: The paper formalizes oscillations of Markov jump processes via the ratio Q of oscillation frequency to decay rate, and derives a spectral/kinetic counting bound: the number of oscillations with ratio exceeding Q is bounded by 2(d-1)/(πQ). It shows that nested-cycle network topologies saturate (approach) this bound, and uses the bound as an inverse inference tool to infer hidden system size from observed oscillations.
AI.result: A d-state system sustains fewer than 2(d-1)/(πQ) oscillations whose frequency-to-decay ratio exceeds Q; nested cycles approach this bound, and the measured oscillations reveal the minimum size of an unobserved hidden system.
AI.conclusion: The work supplies the missing Weyl-type counting law for stochastic jump systems, trading the sharp quantum count d(d-1)/2 for a Q-dependent damped bound; this yields a practical criterion for inferring hidden degrees of freedom from observed oscillatory decay.

title: Experimental visual quantum state discrimination
summary: Almost all solutions to vision tasks $\unicode{x2014}$ offered by nature and technology alike $\unicode{x2014}$ rely on capturing an image using a lens or a similar optical instrument, followed by computational analysis by neurons of a brain or a digital computer. This approach is inherently suboptimal in photon-limited and noisy conditions, where critical information is irreversibly lost at the measurement stage. We address this gap by introducing AI-driven optimization of quantum measurements on the incoming photons, learning how to extract the maximum possible information for a given computer vision task from each incoming photon. The trained measurement consists of a diffractive optical neural network (DONN) followed by a detector array. We train the DONN with a quantum information-theoretic objective that maximizes the rate at which the discrimination error decays as photons accumulate. The resulting measurement achieves exponentially lower error than both direct imaging and a DONN optimized for single-photon discrimination. We validate the advantage in a noiseless setting as well as a photon-counting experiment with an electron-multiplying CCD with the noise corresponding to $10^4$ photons per single signal photon, where the measurement also learns to mitigate the detector noise.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AI-driven optimization of quantum measurements using a diffractive optical neural network (DONN) to maximize information extraction per photon for vision tasks, achieving exponentially lower error than conventional imaging and single-photon-optimized DONNs under photon-limited and noisy conditions.
AI.motivation: Almost all vision solutions (biological and technological) rely on lens-based image capture followed by computational analysis. This approach is inherently suboptimal in photon-limited and noisy conditions because critical information is irreversibly lost at the measurement stage, before computation can exploit it.
AI.method: The authors introduce AI-driven optimization of quantum measurements on incoming photons. The trained measurement consists of a diffractive optical neural network (DONN) followed by a detector array, trained with a quantum information-theoretic objective that maximizes the rate at which discrimination error decays as photons accumulate. Validation includes a noiseless setting and a photon-counting experiment with an electron-multiplying CCD having noise corresponding to 10^4 photons per single signal photon.
AI.result: The resulting measurement achieves exponentially lower error than both direct imaging and a DONN optimized for single-photon discrimination. In the noisy EMCCD experiment, the measurement also learns to mitigate detector noise.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing quantum measurements directly at the photon-capture stage, guided by a quantum information-theoretic objective, yields substantial gains over conventional imaging pipelines for photon-limited vision tasks and can adapt to real detector noise.

title: Practical Ellipse Fitting for Atom Interferometry
summary: In differential atom interferometry, it is necessary to extract the differential phase shift between two interferometers that are individually noisy. A variety of techniques can be used for this purpose, under the general label of ellipse fitting. We compare several methods for ellipse fitting, considering parameters and performance relevant to atom interferometry. Statistical, algebraic, geometric and Bayesian methods are discussed, and we describe a novel "reciprocal" geometric method that offers some benefits. Each method has advantages and disadvantages that depend on the use case required. Supplemental material includes basic Python and Matlab code for each method.

AI.tldr: A comparison of ellipse-fitting methods (statistical, algebraic, geometric, and Bayesian) for extracting the differential phase shift in dual atom interferometers, including a novel "reciprocal" geometric method.
AI.motivation: In differential atom interferometry, the differential phase shift must be recovered from two individually noisy interferometers; ellipse fitting is the standard tool for this, but the relative merits of competing fitting approaches are not well characterized for this application.
AI.method: Several ellipse-fitting methods—statistical, algebraic, geometric, and Bayesian—are compared, evaluated with parameters and performance metrics relevant to atom interferometry. A new "reciprocal" geometric method is introduced and described.
AI.result: Each method shows distinct trade-offs; performance varies with use case. The reciprocal geometric method offers some benefits. Reference Python and Matlab implementations for every method are provided as supplemental material.
AI.conclusion: No single method is universally best: the appropriate choice depends on the specific atom-interferometry use case, and the reciprocal geometric approach is a worthwhile addition to the toolkit.

title: Dynamical Light-Matter Coupling with Protected Superconducting Oscillators
comment: PhD thesis, National University of Singapore, February 2026
summary: Superconducting circuits hosting long-lived bosonic modes are an excellent platform for emulating the dynamics of light and matter and exploiting them for quantum information processing. The space of accessible dynamics is greatly extended by introducing the frequency tunability of artificial atoms, whereby the interactions with the light field of a microwave cavity can be modified on demand. However, using external flux bias to control the frequency of transmons introduces significant losses to coupled cavities, reducing their single-photon lifetimes to a few tens of $μ$s. These imperfections compromise the usefulness of the bosonic mode, which loses its ability to store and manipulate the quantum information of many-photon states. This thesis investigates the issue and demonstrates how to enhance the flux control of microwave cavities without compromising protection. Several hardware solutions were explored, including off-plane remote flux sources routed by a magnetic hose, and lithographically printed on-chip lines equipped with multiple stages of filtering. These developments equip the systems with broadband flux control and photon lifetimes of several hundred $μ$s. They enable the real-time manipulation of the two central parameters of the Rabi model: detuning and coupling strength. This flexibility translates into operational primitives of interest, such as the calibration of nonlinearities to different interaction regimes, the activation of parametric resonances with adjustable coupling strengths, and the use of number-selective transmon-cavity transitions for qudit state preparation and control. These results lay the groundwork for exploring richer synthetic light-matter systems, controlling cavities with more complex nonlinear circuits, and engineering driven-dissipative systems with applications in quantum computation and sensing.

AI.tldr: This thesis addresses flux-control-induced loss in microwave cavities coupled to transmon qubits and demonstrates hardware solutions that restore long photon lifetimes while enabling tunable light-matter interaction for quantum information processing.
AI.motivation: Superconducting circuits with long-lived bosonic modes are strong platforms for emulating light-matter dynamics and quantum information processing. Frequency-tunable artificial atoms extend the accessible dynamics, but using external flux bias to tune transmon frequencies introduces significant losses to coupled cavities, reducing single-photon lifetimes to a few tens of μs and undermining the bosonic mode's ability to store and manipulate many-photon quantum states.
AI.method: The work investigates the loss mechanism and develops hardware solutions to enhance flux control of microwave cavities without compromising protection. Approaches explored include off-plane remote flux sources routed by a magnetic hose, and lithographically printed on-chip lines with multiple stages of filtering.
AI.result: The developed systems achieve broadband flux control together with photon lifetimes of several hundred μs. This enables real-time manipulation of the two central Rabi-model parameters—detuning and coupling strength—supporting operational primitives such as calibration of nonlinearities across interaction regimes, activation of parametric resonances with adjustable coupling strengths, and number-selective transmon-cavity transitions for qudit state preparation and control.
AI.conclusion: The results lay the groundwork for exploring richer synthetic light-matter systems, controlling cavities with more complex nonlinear circuits, and engineering driven-dissipative systems with applications in quantum computation and sensing.

title: Adaptive Protocol for Rényi Entropy Estimation
summary: The second-order Rényi entropy is one of the most important quantities used for characterizing the entanglement structure of states prepared in quantum many-body experiments. With access to qubit projective measurement data, it can be estimated via a protocol in which repeated measurements are taken after each of a set of random local unitary operations is applied to the quantum state. To obtain accurate values for the second Rényi entropy on shot-limited devices, care must be taken when choosing the number of different unitary settings to apply, and the respective number of projective measurements to take. In this paper, we propose an adaptive protocol for estimating the Rényi entropy that iteratively optimizes the ratio of basis settings to measurements, using a gradient-based approach and starting from an initial small set of measurements. Using synthetic data, we demonstrate that for several prototypical states, our method converges to values for this ratio that are comparable to the optimal values obtained by a brute-force grid search, and it exhibits slower growth of the measurement budget required for a fixed target accuracy than fixed-ratio protocols. Our adaptive protocol therefore promotes efficient estimation of the Rényi entropy in finite-size, shot-limited quantum experiments by making effective use of the available measurement budget.

AI.tldr: An adaptive protocol is proposed to estimate the second-order Rényi entropy on shot-limited quantum devices by iteratively optimizing the ratio of random local unitary basis settings to projective measurements, using gradient-based optimization.
AI.motivation: Accurate second-order Rényi entropy estimation on shot-limited devices requires carefully choosing the number of random unitary settings versus projective measurements per setting; fixed-ratio protocols are inefficient in this trade-off.
AI.method: Randomized local unitary measurements followed by projective measurements; an iterative gradient-based optimization adapts the basis-setting-to-measurement ratio, starting from a small initial measurement set. Validated on synthetic data for prototypical states and benchmarked against brute-force grid search and fixed-ratio protocols.
AI.result: The adaptive method converges to ratios comparable to the optimal values found by brute-force grid search, and shows slower growth of the measurement budget required for a fixed target accuracy compared with fixed-ratio protocols.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive protocol enables more efficient Rényi entropy estimation in finite-size, shot-limited quantum experiments by making effective use of the available measurement budget.

title: Realizing Unstructured PDE Forecasting on Superconducting Quantum Processors
summary: Simulating high dimensional unstructured Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) with quantum processors is a major challenge with significant potential benefit. Existing methods have been demonstrated at small qubit counts, on simplifications of realistic problems. We implement a quantum reservoir network (QRN) for forecasting high-dimensional unstructured PDEs using up to 52 qubits on IBM superconducting hardware. Our method is gradient-free and does not suffer from the challenges of variational quantum algorithms. Instead, the QRN provides a large kernel space, up to 2^52 dimensions and beyond the reach of exact classical simulation, that remains useful under current hardware noise levels. Furthermore, a partial measure-and-reset mechanism enables total circuit runtime for ~24 times the qubit coherence time, so qubit lifetimes do not limit the forecast horizon. Thus, our method enables forecasting realistic unstructured nonlinear PDEs on quantum hardware. Typical difficulties associated with predicting large scale PDEs, such as transpilation, exponential shot requirements, hardware noise, and short qubit lifetimes are mitigated through careful design considerations and a dynamic observable reconstruction method. We validate our approach using a ~34k cell unstructured 2D cylinder flow at Reynolds number 1000 and a challenging nonlinear Gray--Scott reaction--diffusion problem, demonstrating high fidelity prediction on CUDA-Q simulation and on 26 and 52-qubit superconducting quantum processors. Specifically, we show that adding QRN features to an autoencoder linear prediction pipeline reduces prediction error by 21%-43%. Finally, we demonstrate closed-loop autoregressive PDE forecasting on these problems. This work demonstrates, for the first time, quantum circuits with depth beyond qubit lifetimes achieving accurate unstructured mesh forecasting on highly nonlinear PDEs.

AI.tldr: A gradient-free quantum reservoir network forecasts high-dimensional unstructured nonlinear PDEs on up to 52 qubits on IBM superconducting hardware, achieving accurate predictions despite noise and short coherence times by using a large kernel space with partial measure-and-reset to extend runtime beyond qubit lifetimes.
AI.motivation: Simulating high-dimensional unstructured PDEs with quantum processors is challenging but potentially highly beneficial. Existing methods are limited to small qubit counts and simplified problems, and standard variational quantum algorithms suffer from trainability and noise issues on real hardware.
AI.method: The authors implement a gradient-free quantum reservoir network (QRN) exploiting a large kernel space (up to 2^52 dimensions, beyond exact classical simulation) that remains useful under hardware noise. A partial measure-and-reset mechanism enables total circuit runtime ~24 times the qubit coherence time, decoupling forecast horizon from qubit lifetimes. They mitigate transpilation, exponential shot requirements, noise, and short coherence via careful design plus a dynamic observable reconstruction method. QRN features are integrated into an autoencoder linear prediction pipeline for closed-loop autoregressive forecasting.
AI.result: Validated on a ~34k cell unstructured 2D cylinder flow at Reynolds number 1000 and a nonlinear Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion problem, showing high-fidelity prediction on CUDA-Q simulation and on 26- and 52-qubit superconducting processors. Adding QRN features to the autoencoder linear prediction pipeline reduces prediction error by 21%–43%. Closed-loop autoregressive forecasting is demonstrated on both problems.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates, for the first time, quantum circuits with depth beyond qubit lifetimes achieving accurate unstructured mesh forecasting on highly nonlinear PDEs, enabling realistic unstructured nonlinear PDE forecasting on current quantum hardware.

title: A trace costs one quantifier: the exact complexity of perfect play in nonlocal games

summary: Given a finite nonlocal game, can the players win with certainty? We prove that the existence of a perfect normal spatial strategy is $Σ^0_2$-complete, even when restricted to games of value one, so it cannot be decided even with an oracle for the halting problem. This is strictly harder than perfect play in the finite-dimensional and commuting-operator models, which are $Σ^0_1$-complete and $Π^0_1$-complete. Within the commuting model, the existence of a perfect normal strategy with a finite or semifinite von Neumann host is $Σ^0_2$-complete, whereas for every fixed type $\mathrm{III}_λ$ subtype it has the same $Π^0_1$-complete language as unrestricted commuting play. A trace thus costs one existential number quantifier: the hardness constructions force every perfect strategy to choose a finite clock period or a finite tree depth. Spatial $Σ^0_2$-completeness also holds when finite entanglement entropy is required, and both forms are formally verified in Lean. For every computable $0<α<1$, perfect spatial play with $\mathrm{Tr}\,h^α<\infty$ for the reduced density $h$ is $Σ^0_2$-complete as well; these conditions form a strict ladder between finite rank and finite entropy. We also prove $Σ^0_2$-completeness for one-shot zero-error communication with normal entanglement, and construct a finite channel with zero-error codes of a given size each of which needs infinite entanglement entropy.

AI.tldr: The existence of a perfect normal spatial strategy for finite nonlocal games is Σ⁰₂-complete (even for value-one games), strictly harder than the finite-dimensional (Σ⁰₁) and commuting-operator (Π⁰₁) models. A trace costs exactly one existential number quantifier. The exact-entropy and Tr h^α conditions form a strict ladder between finite rank and finite entropy, and analogous Σ⁰₂-completeness holds for one-shot zero-error communication.
AI.motivation: Decidability of perfect winning in nonlocal games is well understood for the finite-dimensional and commuting-operator models, but the spatial (tensor-product) model with normal (von Neumann algebraic) strategies is left open. The paper aims to characterize the exact computational complexity of perfect spatial play and to quantify how allowing infinite-dimensional/traced resources changes decidability relative to the commuting model.
AI.method: Reductions establishing completeness for the arithmetical hierarchy: constructions forcing every perfect strategy to commit to a finite clock period or a finite tree depth, thereby introducing exactly one existential number quantifier (Σ⁰₂). The analysis is stratified across host von Neumann algebra types (finite, semifinite, and fixed type III_λ), extended to entropy constraints (finite entropy, exact Tr h^α < ∞ for computable 0<α<1), and to one-shot zero-error channel coding. Key hardness results are formally verified in Lean.
AI.result: Perfect normal spatial strategies are Σ⁰₂-complete, even restricted to value-one games, hence undecidable even with a halting oracle. Within the commuting model, perfect strategies over finite or semifinite hosts are Σ⁰₂-complete, while each fixed type III_λ subtype yields the same Π⁰₁-complete language as unrestricted commuting play. Spatial Σ⁰₂-completeness also holds under finite entanglement entropy and under Tr h^α<∞ for every computable 0<α<1; these conditions form a strict ladder between finite rank and finite entropy. Σ⁰₂-completeness extends to one-shot zero-error communication with normal entanglement, and a finite channel is constructed whose zero-error codes of a given size each require infinite entanglement entropy.
AI.conclusion: Spatial perfect play is strictly harder than both finite-dimensional and commuting-operator perfect play, sitting one quantifier higher (Σ⁰₂), with the cost concretely attributable to the trace. Type III_λ hosts recover the Π⁰₁ commuting language, while finite/semifinite hosts and entropy-bounded variants are Σ⁰₂-complete, yielding a strict hierarchy from finite rank through Tr h^α to finite entropy. These results transfer to one-shot zero-error communication and separate finite from infinite-entropy resources, with central hardness arguments machine-checked in Lean.

title: On the estimation of linear-optical amplitudes and probabilities with entangled input state
summary: Most proposed applications of boson samplers, including photonic machine-learning models, do not use the samples themselves but estimates of output probabilities, marginals or overlaps, obtained to additive precision from a finite number of shots. For product inputs such as single photons, these quantities can already be estimated classically with Gurvits's algorithm and its generalisations. We ask whether entangled inputs change this picture. For any $n$-photon input that is a matrix-product state of bond dimension $χ$, with one photon per site and $L$ modes per site, we give an unbiased estimator of any output amplitude of an $m$-mode interferometer, whose mean-square error after $N$ draws is at most $\|ψ\|^2/N$ whatever the interferometer, the output pattern and the entanglement of the state. Each draw costs $O(nLχ^2+nL^3+mn)$ operations after $O(nLχ^3)$ preprocessing, and an additive error $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-δ$ requires $O(\|ψ\|^2\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/δ))$ draws, with memory of the order of the input size. The main application is to light emitted sequentially by quantum emitters, such as spin-based sources of photonic cluster states, for which $χ$ is bounded by the dimension of the source's retained quantum memory: one spin gives $χ=2$ at any length, and a memory of $k$ qubits, held in emitters or in photons stored in a delay line, gives $χ\le2^k$, so the cost stays polynomial as long as $k=O(\log n)$. The same sampler also estimates traced-memory probabilities, overlaps and individual marginal probabilities. All guarantees are additive: the estimator gives neither relative estimates of exponentially small probabilities nor a sampler of the output distribution.

AI.tldr: Entangled (matrix-product-state) inputs do not fundamentally restore quantum advantage for estimating boson-sampler output amplitudes: an efficient unbiased estimator with additive-error guarantees exists, at cost polynomial in the source's retained memory.
AI.motivation: Most proposed boson-sampler applications (e.g., photonic machine learning) use estimated output probabilities, marginals, or overlaps to additive precision rather than the samples themselves. For product inputs like single photons, Gurvits's algorithm already estimates these classically. The paper asks whether entangled inputs change this classical-simulability picture.
AI.method: For any n-photon input that is a matrix-product state of bond dimension χ (one photon per site, L modes per site), the authors construct an unbiased estimator of any output amplitude of an m-mode interferometer. Each draw costs O(nLχ²+nL³+mn) operations after O(nLχ³) preprocessing; memory is on the order of the input size. The estimator also extends to traced-memory probabilities, overlaps, and individual marginal probabilities.
AI.result: The mean-square error after N draws is at most ‖ψ‖²/N for any interferometer, output pattern, and input entanglement. Achieving additive error ε with probability ≥1−δ requires O(‖ψ‖²ε⁻²log(1/δ)) draws. For light emitted sequentially by quantum emitters (e.g., spin-based photonic cluster-state sources), χ is bounded by the retained quantum memory: one spin gives χ=2 at any length, and k memory qubits give χ≤2^k, keeping cost polynomial while k=O(log n).
AI.conclusion: All guarantees are additive: the estimator yields neither relative estimates of exponentially small probabilities nor a true sampler of the output distribution. Entangled MPS inputs with bounded retained memory thus remain classically estimable to additive precision, limiting the advantage for applications relying only on such estimates.

title: Delta-Corrected Shot Reduction for Bypassing Optimization Plateaus in Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
summary: The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) remains a cornerstone hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for quantum simulation, yet its scalability is fundamentally constrained by heavy measurement overheads. While strategies such as variance-preserved shot reduction (VPSR) mitigates this cost, they suffer from convergence instability and optimization stagnation caused by finite-sample bias in limited pilot shots. To overcome this limitation, we introduce delta-corrected shot reduction (DCSR), an analytically enhanced shot allocation strategy that rigorously mitigates finite-sample instability. Utilizing the multivariate delta method, we derive explicit higher-order bias correction terms for the empirical reduction factor. Both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations reveal that incorporating higher-order statistical moments, such as skewness and kurtosis, provides the gradient resolution necessary to bypass noise-induced barren plateaus. DSCR significantly accelerates convergence compared to standard VPSR across diverse noise and resource regimes while matching or decreasing cumulative measurement costs, establishing a mathematically rigorous framework for variance-stabilized shot allocation on near-term hardware.

AI.tldr: DCSR is an analytically bias-corrected shot-allocation strategy for VQE that uses the multivariate delta method to remove finite-sample bias, enabling faster, more stable convergence than VPSR at equal or lower measurement cost.
AI.motivation: VQE is a cornerstone of quantum simulation but its scalability is limited by heavy measurement overheads. Variance-preserved shot reduction (VPSR) reduces this cost but suffers from convergence instability and optimization stagnation due to finite-sample bias arising from limited pilot shots.
AI.method: The authors introduce delta-corrected shot reduction (DCSR), extending VPSR by deriving explicit higher-order bias-correction terms for the empirical reduction factor via the multivariate delta method. These corrections incorporate higher-order statistical moments such as skewness and kurtosis.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations show that the higher-order moments provide the gradient resolution needed to bypass noise-induced barren plateaus. DCSR significantly accelerates convergence versus standard VPSR across diverse noise and resource regimes while matching or decreasing cumulative measurement costs.
AI.conclusion: DCSR provides a mathematically rigorous framework for variance-stabilized shot allocation suitable for near-term quantum hardware.

title: QAOA Inside ADMM: Subproblem Wins Do Not Become Decomposition Wins at Matched Budgets
summary: We benchmark the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) as the binary subproblem solver in a two-block alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for mixed-binary problems against classical solvers under matched budgets. With 23 optimizer evaluations per subproblem, scoring determines the comparison: on its final readout, the optimized QAOA loses to random search at $n=12$ and 16 binary variables (inconclusive at 20; exploratory and post hoc tests). When credited with its best sample, it wins. In a noiseless 12-qubit simulation, transferred-angle depth-2 QAOA finds the exact optimum of 97.3\% of planted-family subproblems, against 50.6\%--67.4\% for the four strongest local heuristics (100\% against 90.4\%--94.4\% crediting the four best bitstrings) and a not significantly different 96.5\% for semidefinite rounding with local search (SDP+LS). Under our evaluation-counting convention, its time to solution there is a factor of three to five below the local heuristics' but grows with a larger exponent; it is ten times that of SDP+LS and, in seconds, 54 times that of tabu search with restarts. For the benchmark class, an unconstrained binary quadratic problem in disguise, ADMM's binary step is a proximal step on the reduced problem: at unit penalty ADMM re-solves it, and for larger penalties exact solutions increasingly stall. On two families that do not reduce to one, less accurate solvers found the problem optimum more often at unit and larger penalties. No family gave QAOA a better ADMM outcome than the best classical solver and penalty. The benchmark includes a correctness gate and a log of its hypothesis tests.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks QAOA as the binary subproblem solver inside a two-block ADMM for mixed-binary problems against classical solvers under matched evaluation budgets, finding QAOA does not yield better ADMM outcomes than the best classical solver and penalty on any tested family.
AI.motivation: QAOA is frequently proposed as a solver for binary subproblems within decomposition methods such as ADMM, but its practical value relative to classical solvers under fair, matched budgets is unclear. The authors aim to test whether QAOA, used as the binary step in ADMM, can outperform strong classical solvers under identical evaluation budgets.
AI.method: QAOA is used as the binary subproblem solver in a two-block ADMM for mixed-binary problems, compared against classical solvers under matched budgets (23 optimizer evaluations per subproblem). Evaluation uses both final-readout scoring and best-sample scoring, with a noiseless 12-qubit simulation, transferred-angle depth-2 QAOA on planted-family subproblems, and comparisons against four strong local heuristics, SDP+LS, and tabu search with restarts. Analysis includes a correctness gate and a log of hypothesis tests, plus studies of the reduced problem structure (unconstrained binary quadratic form) and penalty behavior.
AI.result: On final readout, optimized QAOA loses to random search at n=12 and 16 (inconclusive at 20; exploratory/post hoc). When credited with its best sample, it wins. In noiseless 12-qubit simulation, transferred-angle depth-2 QAOA finds the exact optimum of 97.3% of planted-family subproblems vs 50.6%–67.4% for the four strongest local heuristics (100% vs 90.4%–94.4% when crediting best bitstrings), statistically tied with SDP+LS (96.5%). Its time to solution is 3–5x lower than local heuristics but grows with a larger exponent; about 10x that of SDP+LS and, in seconds, 54x that of tabu search with restarts. The benchmark ADMM binary step is a proximal step on a reduced unconstrained binary quadratic problem: at unit penalty ADMM re-solves it, and larger penalties stall exact solutions. On two non-reducible families, less accurate solvers found the optimum more often. No family gave QAOA a better ADMM outcome than the best classical solver and penalty.
AI.conclusion: Under matched budgets, QAOA as an ADMM binary subproblem solver does not deliver better ADMM outcomes than the best classical solver and penalty on any benchmark family. Its gains are scoring-dependent (best-sample credit) and limited by unfavorable scaling, while classical and hybrid solvers (SDP+LS, tabu search) remain competitive or superior, especially when the binary step reduces to a proximal step on a binary quadratic problem.

title: Beyond the Mean Gap: What Transferred-Angle QAOA Retains on a Superconducting Processor
summary: Hardware executions of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) are often validated by comparing the device's mean cost with a simulation, a check that can miss what matters for optimization. Under global depolarization, the mean normalized gap and the floor-corrected probability of every set of bitstrings, the optimum included, retain the same fraction of their noiseless improvement over uniform sampling. We test this prediction with depth-2, transferred-angle QAOA circuits for binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition on the IBM Heron processor \texttt{ibm\_marrakesh}, with and without dynamical decoupling and twirling. At 12 qubits, the main-family circuits retained 29\% to 46\% of their mean-gap improvement but only 5\% to 15\% of their probability of the optimum, lower on at least nine of ten instances per run. Near-optimal bitstrings were lost about as much as the optimum, whereas the avoidance of poor bitstrings was retained best. In the first submission, a device-matched noise model reproduced the pattern but overestimated the retention of the optimum five- to eightfold. On a rugged planted family, the device found the optimum in 62\% of 768-shot blocks (noiseless: 98\%), within the range of local heuristics. Validations of optimization circuits should report retention of the optimum and of near-optimal sets.

AI.tldr: Under global depolarizing noise, mean gap and floor-corrected bitstring probabilities should retain equal fractions of their noiseless improvement; hardware tests on IBM Heron show this symmetry breaks, with optimum-probability retention far below mean-gap retention, so validation must report optimum and near-optimal retention.
AI.motivation: Standard QAOA hardware validation compares the device's mean cost with simulation, which can obscure what actually matters for optimization. The authors seek to test whether the theoretically predicted uniform retention of information (mean gap vs. optimum probability) holds on real hardware, and to identify which metrics are diagnostic.
AI.method: Theoretical prediction derived under global depolarization: mean normalized gap and floor-corrected probabilities of any bitstring set retain the same fraction of noiseless improvement over uniform sampling. Empirical test: depth-2 transferred-angle QAOA on binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition, run on IBM Heron (ibm_marrakesh), with/without dynamical decoupling and twirling; comparison against a device-matched noise model and a rugged planted-solution family with 768-shot blocks.
AI.result: At 12 qubits, main-family circuits retained 29–46% of mean-gap improvement but only 5–15% of the probability of the optimum, lower on at least 9 of 10 instances per run. Near-optimal bitstrings were lost about as much as the optimum; avoidance of poor bitstrings was retained best. The device-matched noise model reproduced the pattern but overestimated optimum retention 5–8 times. On the rugged planted family, the device found the optimum in 62% of 768-shot blocks vs. 98% noiseless, within the range of local heuristics.
AI.conclusion: The global-depolarization prediction fails empirically: mean-gap retention overstates retention of the optimum and near-optimal sets. Mean-cost validation is therefore insufficient; optimization-circuit validations should explicitly report retention of the optimum and of near-optimal bitstring sets.

title: Compact Quantum Channel Attention for Static ASL Recognition: A Controlled Study with Parameter-Matched Baselines
summary: Hybrid quantum-classical models often report good accuracy on image tasks, but it is rarely clear whether the quantum part is responsible. This paper proposes QCA-DenseNet, a static American Sign Language (ASL) recognition pipeline in which an eight-qubit variational circuit acts as a channel-attention gate on DenseNet121 features. The quantum channel attention (QCA) gate has 17,464 parameters, 7.51 times fewer than a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) block. The pipeline is tested on 1,815 MU HandImages images by holding out one of five signers at a time, and a frozen-backbone ablation uses small parts of the Kaggle ASL Alphabet data. On unseen signers, QCA-DenseNet reaches 94.50% mean accuracy, above SE (93.72%) and within 0.28 points of the best model. A matched classical MLP and a model without attention perform about the same, and no difference is significant. QCA gives a much smaller attention gate without a detectable loss in accuracy, but no quantum advantage.

AI.tldr: QCA-DenseNet uses an 8-qubit variational circuit as a channel-attention gate on DenseNet121 features for static ASL recognition; it matches SE-based attention with far fewer parameters but shows no quantum advantage.
AI.motivation: Hybrid quantum-classical models often report high image-task accuracy, but it is rarely clear whether the quantum component is actually responsible. The authors aim to isolate and test that claim with a controlled comparison.
AI.method: A static ASL recognition pipeline in which an eight-qubit variational circuit serves as a channel-attention gate (QCA) on DenseNet121 features. The gate has 17,464 parameters, 7.51x fewer than a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) block. Evaluated on 1,815 MU HandImages with leave-one-signer-out (5 folds), plus a frozen-backbone ablation using small subsets of Kaggle ASL Alphabet; controls include SE, a matched classical MLP gate, and a no-attention model.
AI.result: On unseen signers, QCA-DenseNet reaches 94.50% mean accuracy vs 93.72% for SE, within 0.28 points of the best model. The matched classical MLP and no-attention model perform about the same, and no difference is statistically significant.
AI.conclusion: The quantum gate yields a much smaller attention module without a detectable accuracy loss, but provides no quantum advantage; the ablation indicates the quantum part is not the source of performance.

title: Initialization masks overcome decoding obstructions in compressed QAOA
summary: In compressed quantum optimization, a variational state is converted into a classical assignment by decoding noncommuting observables. We show that this step creates structural restrictions that changing the initialization can remove, even when increasing circuit depth cannot. For an explicit infinite family of connected cubic graphs on $n=3r$ vertices, with a fixed Pauli encoding and deterministic sign decoder, every all-plus QAOA circuit has cut at most $2r$, at every finite depth and every real angle sequence. A uniform signed product-state mask at fixed depth-one angles has expected cut $13r/4$, an additive advantage $5n/12$; an infinite subfamily admits an optimal mask. A second construction retains a linear depth-one separation under weak weighted couplings, a bounded cost-angle domain and a specified production-encoder ordering. Noiseless simulations then test classical mask selection before energy optimization. On 1,699 random cubic MaxCut instances, one selected mask achieves mean ratio $0.9100$, versus $0.7067$ for the all-plus $X$ baseline and $0.9125$ for the best of $r^2$ separately optimized random masks. On complete cohorts of weighted MaxCut, sparse Ising, Max-2-XOR and Max-2-SAT, the selected mask also improves on the baseline at every size, but it trails the pool at small sizes and leads it significantly only at the larger MaxCut and Ising sizes. Finite-pool order statistics separate the effect of selection from that of drawing a random mask. The results distinguish decoded expressivity from optimized energy and empirical performance; they do not establish a quantum computational advantage.

AI.tldr: Changing the product-state initialization of a QAOA circuit can yield a linear cut advantage that circuit depth cannot, because the classical decoding step imposes structural limits on all-plus circuits.
AI.motivation: In compressed quantum optimization, decoding noncommuting observables into a classical assignment imposes structural restrictions. The authors aim to show these restrictions are removable via initialization rather than depth, distinguishing decoded expressivity from optimized energy and empirical performance.
AI.method: Construct an explicit infinite family of connected cubic graphs on n=3r vertices with fixed Pauli encoding and deterministic sign decoder. Prove an upper bound of 2r for all-plus QAOA at any finite depth and any real angle sequence, then analyze a uniform signed product-state mask at fixed depth-one angles (expected cut 13r/4, advantage 5n/12), including an optimal-mask subfamily and a weak-weighted-coupling variant with bounded cost-angle domain and specified production-encoder ordering. Validate with noiseless simulations and finite-pool order statistics.
AI.result: All-plus QAOA achieves cut at most 2r versus expected 13r/4 for the mask, an additive advantage of 5n/12. On 1,699 random cubic MaxCut instances, a selected mask reaches mean ratio 0.9100 vs 0.7067 for the all-plus X baseline and 0.9125 for best of r^2 separately optimized random masks. Across complete cohorts (weighted MaxCut, sparse Ising, Max-2-XOR, Max-2-SAT) the selected mask beats the baseline at every size, trails the pool at small sizes, and leads significantly only at larger MaxCut and Ising sizes.
AI.conclusion: Initialization, not depth, can overcome decoding-induced structural restrictions, establishing a provable depth-one separation. Results separate decoded expressivity from optimized energy and empirical performance, and do not establish a quantum computational advantage.

title: Simulating the quantum switch with quantum circuits is impossible
comment: 34 pages pages, 14 figures. All comments are welcome, feel free to get in touch via email
summary: The quantum switch is a higher-order transformation that combines input quantum channels in an indefinite causal order. Whether quantum circuits can simulate its action, and how many calls to the input channels such a simulation requires, are natural questions about the power of quantum control of causal order. In this work, we prove that no quantum circuit with classically controlled causal order can exactly and deterministically simulate the quantum switch for arbitrary input channels using any finite number of calls. This impossibility holds already for qubit channels and extends to the complete $r$-switch, which coherently controls all permutations of $r$ input channels. These results settle the question of exact deterministic circuit simulation of the quantum switch. They demonstrate that processes with indefinite causal order cannot, in general, be efficiently simulated in this setting even by quantum circuits with classically controlled causal order.

AI.tldr: No quantum circuit with classically controlled causal order can exactly and deterministically simulate the quantum switch for arbitrary input channels using any finite number of calls, even for qubit channels, and this extends to the complete r-switch.
AI.motivation: The quantum switch combines channels in indefinite causal order; it is natural to ask whether its action can be simulated by quantum circuits, and how many calls to input channels such a simulation requires, as a probe of the power of quantum control of causal order.
AI.method: A proof-based approach establishing an impossibility: showing that no classically controlled causal order circuit can exactly and deterministically reproduce the quantum switch's action for arbitrary input channels with any finite number of calls, with the argument holding already at the level of qubit channels and generalized to the complete r-switch (coherently controlling all permutations of r channels).
AI.result: Exact deterministic simulation of the quantum switch by classically controlled causal order circuits is impossible with any finite number of calls, even restricted to qubit channels; the result extends to the complete r-switch.
AI.conclusion: Processes with indefinite causal order cannot in general be efficiently simulated in this setting, even by quantum circuits with classically controlled causal order; these results settle the question of exact deterministic circuit simulation of the quantum switch.

title: A Grover-Amplified Oracle for Maximum Clique on Graph, Minimum Hitting set and Dualizations on Hypergraphs Built on Quantum Phase Estimation
summary: In this paper, we use a quantum circuit called the Graph Encoding Operator which, applied to the complement $\bar G$ of any graph $G$, yields an oracle for the maximum clique problem suitable for amplification via Grover's algorithm. Analogously, we devise a Hypergraph Encoding Operator which, when applied to a hypergraph $\mathcal H$, yields an oracle for the minimum hitting set suitable for amplification via Grover's algorithm. Interestingly, the latter oracle provides, when measured, an approximation of the number of hitting sets of the hypergraph, thus solving the dualization problem for positive Boolean functions represented in a positive irredundant disjunctive normal form. We give the full construction of both operators, prove their correctness, analyze their complexity, and provide an implementation on a quantum simulator. We discuss the resulting complexity, contrast them with existing quantum computer algorithms based on Grover search and we will show that our algorithms outperform, to the best of our knowledge, all of the previous algorithms on space computational complexity by requiring only $O(N)$ number of qubits with respect to the number of vertices $N$, for representing both graphs and hypergraphs in the encoding operator and, consequently, results in an oracle for both graphs and hypergraphs that uses only $O(N)$ qubits even when the hypergraph contains an exponential (on the number of vertices) number of hyperedges.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Graph Encoding and Hypergraph Encoding quantum operators that build Grover-amplifiable oracles for maximum clique and minimum hitting set, requiring only O(N) qubits, and shows the hitting-set oracle also approximates the number of hitting sets (solving positive Boolean function dualization).
AI.motivation: Existing quantum algorithms based on Grover search for maximum clique and minimum hitting set impose high space complexity, particularly when the hypergraph has exponentially many hyperedges. The authors aim to reduce the qubit overhead of the encoding/oracle construction.
AI.method: A Graph Encoding Operator applied to the complement complement G of a graph G produces an oracle for maximum clique suitable for Grover amplification. Analogously, a Hypergraph Encoding Operator applied to a hypergraph H produces an oracle for minimum hitting set. The authors give full constructions of both operators, prove correctness, analyze complexity, and implement them on a quantum simulator; the hypergraph oracle, when measured, approximates the number of hitting sets, thereby addressing dualization of positive Boolean functions in positive irredundant DNF.
AI.result: Both oracles are constructed with complexity analysis and simulator validation. The approach uses only O(N) qubits for representing both graphs and hypergraphs in the encoding operator, and the resulting oracles use O(N) qubits even when the hypergraph contains an exponential number of hyperedges; the algorithms outperform prior Grover-based quantum algorithms on space complexity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed encoding operators yield space-efficient Grover-amplifiable oracles for maximum clique and minimum hitting set, achieving O(N) qubit usage and improving on previous quantum approaches in space complexity, while additionally providing a route to approximate hitting-set counting and positive Boolean function dualization.

title: Demonstration of a partial knowledge quantum key distribution protocol
summary: We demonstrate a novel QKD protocol, named \texttt{Bridge[$d,q$]}, which generalizes the \texttt{SARG04} protocol to $d$ dimensions and $q$ bases. In this protocol, Alice and Bob gain only partial knowledge about each other's raw key. Nevertheless, this partial information is sufficient to distill a definite mutual encryption key. We present an experimental demonstration of the \texttt{Bridge[$2,3$]} protocol. The three unbiased polarization bases were switched using a single Pockels cell. The applied polarization basis switching method is relevant to any 3-basis QKD protocol and to other applications that require fast manipulation of photon polarization qubits.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a generalized QKD protocol, Bridge[d,q], extending SARG04 to d dimensions and q bases, and experimentally demonstrates Bridge[2,3] using a single Pockels cell for rapid three-basis polarization switching.
AI.motivation: Standard QKD protocols require Alice and Bob to hold matching raw-key knowledge, and experimental basis manipulation (especially multi-basis switching) is challenging. The authors seek a protocol where only partial mutual knowledge suffices to distill a secure key and a practical, fast polarization basis-switching method.
AI.method: A generalized QKD protocol, Bridge[d,q], is formulated as a d-dimensional, q-basis extension of SARG04. An experimental demonstration of Bridge[2,3] is performed by switching three unbiased polarization bases using a single Pockels cell.
AI.result: Alice and Bob, despite having only partial knowledge of each other's raw key, distill a definite mutual encryption key. The three-basis switching is achieved with a single Pockels cell, enabling fast polarization qubit manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Partial mutual information is sufficient for secure key distillation in the Bridge[d,q] framework. The single-Pockels-cell switching technique applies to any 3-basis QKD protocol and other applications requiring fast control of photon polarization qubits.

title: From Machine-Discovered Graphs to Analytic NOON State Families
summary: Machine-discovered graphs generate NOON states after heralding and output-number selection, but their interference mechanisms and optical implementations are not immediately apparent. We derive analytic weight conditions for arbitrary photon number $N$ by counting pair-generation processes that cancel mixed output occupations. These conditions yield quantum experiments by path identity using a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometer and photon-pair sources. Takagi decomposition of the pair-amplitude matrix gives an exact Gaussian implementation using single-mode squeezers followed by a passive interferometer. Any pure, zero-displacement Gaussian scheme with photon-number-resolved heralding requires at least $N-2$ herald photons, and both constructions attain this bound. At finite gain, the ideal Takagi implementation maintains unit fidelity after output-number selection, whereas fidelity decreases in path identity with fixed source settings.

AI.tldr: Machine-discovered graphs that herald NOON states are given analytic weight conditions for arbitrary photon number N, plus two optical implementations: a Hong-Ou-Mandel path-identity scheme and an exact Gaussian (Takagi) scheme using squeezers and a passive interferometer, both meeting an N-2 herald-photon bound.
AI.motivation: Machine-discovered graphs can generate NOON states after heralding and output-number selection, but their interference mechanisms and physical optical implementations are not immediately apparent, so a principled understanding and realizable construction are needed.
AI.method: Derives analytic weight conditions for arbitrary photon number N by counting pair-generation processes that cancel mixed output occupations. These conditions yield quantum experiments via path identity using a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometer and photon-pair sources. A Takagi decomposition of the pair-amplitude matrix gives an exact Gaussian implementation with single-mode squeezers followed by a passive interferometer. Also proves a lower bound of at least N-2 herald photons for any pure, zero-displacement Gaussian scheme with photon-number-resolved heralding.
AI.result: The analytic weight conditions specify which graphs herald NOON states, both constructions attain the N-2 herald-photon bound, and at finite gain the ideal Takagi implementation keeps unit fidelity after output-number selection while the path-identity scheme's fidelity degrades with fixed source settings.
AI.conclusion: The work clarifies the interference mechanism behind machine-discovered NOON-state graphs, provides two concrete optical implementations, establishes an N-2 herald-photon bound that both schemes achieve, and identifies the Takagi/Gaussian construction as the robust choice at finite gain due to its unit fidelity under output-number selection.

title: Hidden Coherence and Controlled Quasihole Motion in a Fermionic Laughlin State on a Superconducting Quantum Processor
comment: Main text: 8 pages, 4 figures; Supplemental Material: 17 pages, 8 figures
summary: Fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states support fractionalized excitations and geometric phases, yet experimentally resolving the many-body coherence encoded in their wave functions remains challenging. Here, we prepare a three-electron $ν=1/3$ Laughlin state on the Haldane sphere using seven superconducting qubits and reconstruct its many-body density matrix. Through Read's composite-boson construction, we reveal vortex-dressed coherence that remains appreciable over a larger separation range than electron coherence. The extended profile is suppressed in a Fock-diagonal reference constructed from the measured populations, demonstrating its dependence on off-diagonal many-body coherence. We further prepare a one-flux-added quasihole and characterize its fractional charge response against finite-size benchmarks. Controlled quasihole motion yields an effective geometric-phase signature from the reconstructed dominant-eigenstate trajectory. These complementary measurements provide microscopic access to the coherent structure and quasihole response of a finite fermionic Laughlin state, demonstrating an experimental route to probing strongly correlated FQH wave functions on programmable quantum processors.

AI.tldr: Three-electron ν=1/3 Laughlin state prepared on a Haldane sphere with seven superconducting qubits, with full many-body density matrix reconstruction revealing vortex-dressed composite-boson coherence and quasihole fractional-charge and geometric-phase responses.
AI.motivation: Fractional quantum Hall states host fractionalized excitations and geometric phases, but experimentally resolving the many-body coherence encoded in their wave functions remains challenging.
AI.method: Prepare a three-electron ν=1/3 Laughlin state on the Haldane sphere using seven superconducting qubits and reconstruct its many-body density matrix. Use Read's composite-boson construction to extract vortex-dressed coherence, benchmark against a Fock-diagonal reference built from measured populations, add one flux to create a quasihole, and drive controlled quasihole motion to extract an effective geometric-phase signature from the dominant-eigenstate trajectory.
AI.result: Vortex-dressed coherence extends over a larger separation range than electron coherence and is suppressed in the Fock-diagonal reference, confirming its dependence on off-diagonal many-body coherence; the quasihole shows a fractional-charge response consistent with finite-size benchmarks, and its motion yields an effective geometric-phase signature.
