AI.method: Starting from a driven three-level system, they derive an effective two-level description with nonequilibrium stationary populations, then apply a quantum central limit approach to obtain collective Langevin dynamics. From the same microscopic stationary state they compute the electromagnetic susceptibility and quantum noise-current correlations, linking them to the reservoir operators of conventional macroscopic QED.
AI.result: Optical response is governed by the population difference, whereas noise correlations depend separately on the populations of the two levels. At optical transparency the imaginary part of the susceptibility vanishes while quantum fluctuations remain finite. The noise statistics are interpreted via an effective reservoir occupation and a purification with two vacuum modes, yielding an effective-temperature fluctuation–dissipation relation. Residual fluctuations at transparency can produce finite heating of a nearby quantum probe.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a consistent microscopic underpinning for macroscopic QED in active media, with susceptibility and noise derived from a single stationary state, and predicts observable consequences—finite quantum fluctuations and probe heating at transparency—that distinguish active from passive media.

title: A geometrical approach for obtaining exact analytical solutions for a scalar field in a one-dimensional dynamical cavity
summary: The dynamical Casimir effect was first predicted by G. T. Moore in 1969, who considered a real scalar field inside a cavity with a moving mirror in ($1+1$)D, satisfying Dirichlet boundary conditions. Moore wrote the general solution for the field in terms of a function that satisfies a functional equation nowadays known as the Moore equation.In the literature, exact analytical solutions to the Moore equation form a rather small set, restricted to specific classes of laws of motion. Cole and Schieve (1995) developed a geometrical approach that yielded a general formula for the solution of the Moore equation for cavities initially at rest. However, its application has always been done through numerical calculations, and their approach has therefore long been regarded solely as a numerical method. In this work, we show that their method can also be employed as a powerful method for deriving exact analytical solutions, and show the applicability of this approach to deriving analytical solutions to the Moore equation. We obtain original exact analytical solutions for an expanding cavity with a uniformly moving mirror, a contracting cavity with a mirror that approaches the static one asymptotically, and, in addition, we recover the first analytical solution to the Moore equation for a resonant mirror motion, originally obtained by Law in 1994. Moreover, we extend the Cole-Schieve approach, showing that exact solutions can be constructed from any spacetime region where the Moore function has already been determined. We show that this extended geometrical approach allows us to expand the set of known analytical solutions to the Moore equation from the few classes of motion reported in the literature to an infinite set, as it enables the treatment of new classes of laws of motion obtained by combining those presented here with each other as well as with previously known classes of trajectories.

AI.tldr: The Cole–Schieve geometrical approach, long viewed only as a numerical tool, is shown to be a powerful method for deriving exact analytical solutions of the Moore equation, yielding new closed-form solutions and, via an extension of the method, an infinite set of analytical solutions.
AI.motivation: Exact analytical solutions to the Moore equation, which governs the dynamical Casimir effect for a scalar field in a (1+1)D cavity with a moving Dirichlet mirror, are scarce and restricted to a few specific classes of mirror motion. Although Cole and Schieve (1995) provided a general geometrical formula for cavities initially at rest, its use had always been numerical, so it was regarded purely as a numerical method, leaving many laws of motion without closed-form treatment.
AI.method: The authors reinterpret the Cole–Schieve geometrical construction as an analytical technique. They apply it to derive exact solutions for an expanding cavity with a uniformly moving mirror, a contracting cavity whose mirror approaches the static one asymptotically, and they re-derive Law's (1994) resonant-motion solution. They then extend the geometrical approach so that exact solutions can be constructed starting from any spacetime region in which the Moore function is already known.
AI.result: Original exact analytical solutions are obtained for a uniformly expanding cavity, for a contracting cavity with an asymptotically approaching mirror, and Law's resonant solution is recovered. The extended geometrical approach shows that analytical solutions can be generated by combining these laws of motion with one another and with previously known classes of trajectories.
AI.conclusion: The Cole–Schieve method is not merely numerical but a systematic generator of exact analytical solutions to the Moore equation. The extension presented expands the known analytical solutions from a small finite set of motion classes to an infinite set, enabling treatment of a broad range of new mirror trajectories relevant to the dynamical Casimir effect.

title: Proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture: An Exposition
summary:
We give an exposition of a recent proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, which states that every degree-$d$ polynomial $p : \{0,1\}^n \to [0,1]$ has a variable of influence at least $\mathrm{poly}(\mathrm{Var}(p)/d)$. This implies that quantum query algorithms for decision problems can be efficiently simulated classically on most inputs. It also yields a near-equivalence between the status of the $\mathsf{BPP}$ vs. $\mathsf{BQP}$ problem in the random oracle and unrelativized worlds.
  We organize the proof around four main steps and discuss how each connects to the literature on the analysis of boolean functions and probabilistic combinatorics. To bring out the key ideas, we do not optimize parameters, and our presentation yields weaker exponents than the original.
  $\textbf{Authors' note.}$ The proof was discovered by David Turturean using a research system developed at Physical Superintelligence (PSI), in combination with a non-public Anthropic model. The proof was then shared with the authors, who worked to understand it and prepare this exposition. Anthropic's public models were used in this process.
  The authors did not receive financial compensation from Anthropic or PSI. This article is not intended for publication at a conference or in a journal.

AI.tldr: An expository account of a recent proof of the Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture: every degree-$d$ polynomial $p:\{0,1\}^n\to[0,1]$ has a variable of influence at least $\mathrm{poly}(\mathrm{Var}(p)/d)$, implying efficient classical simulation of quantum query algorithms on most inputs and a near-equivalence of $\mathsf{BPP}$ vs. $\mathsf{BQP}$ in random-oracle and unrelativized worlds; organized into four steps with unoptimized parameters.
AI.motivation: The Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture links the influence of low-degree bounded polynomials to the power of quantum query algorithms, and its resolution has consequences for classical simulation of quantum algorithms and for relativization of $\mathsf{BPP}$ vs. $\mathsf{BQP}$. The paper aims to make the new proof accessible by presenting it in a structured, pedagogical form connecting it to analysis of Boolean functions and probabilistic combinatorics.
AI.method: The authors give an exposition of the proof, organizing it around four main steps, deliberately not optimizing parameters (yielding weaker exponents than the original proof) to foreground the core ideas, and relating each step to existing literature in analysis of Boolean functions and probabilistic combinatorics.
AI.result: The exposition establishes the conjecture's statement — a variable of influence at least $\mathrm{poly}(\mathrm{Var}(p)/d)$ — and derives from it efficient classical simulation of quantum query algorithms for decision problems on most inputs, plus a near-equivalence between the status of $\mathsf{BPP}$ vs. $\mathsf{BQP}$ in the random-oracle and unrelativized worlds, albeit with weaker quantitative bounds than the original proof.
AI.conclusion: The Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture admits a proof, here presented as a four-step exposition with simplified (non-optimized) parameters, connecting the argument to Boolean-function analysis and probabilistic combinatorics; the proof was discovered by David Turturean using a PSI research system with a non-public Anthropic model, and this article is an expository, non-conference work.

title: Pauli propagation in adaptive local frames
summary: The cost of Pauli propagation depends on the local basis in which the evolving operator is expanded. We show that its Pauli complexity splits into an occupation part, invariant under local rotations and bounded from below by the operator mass and length distributions, and a flavour part that a suitable basis can remove. We introduce frame-adaptive Pauli propagation (FAPP), which rotates the basis of every qubit, gate by gate, to the principal axes of the operator's local polarisation, exactly and within the memory structure of Pauli propagation. This simple rule achieves most of what the best local frame can, and the polarisation predicts how much any local frame can gain. In the Ising chain in transverse and longitudinal fields, FAPP lowers the truncation error at fixed memory by up to an order of magnitude and the memory by a size-independent factor of three; on the infinite two-dimensional lattice it needs up to seven times fewer strings for a given certified accuracy, and in Clifford circuits doped with T gates two to eight times fewer.

AI.tldr: FAPP rotates each qubit's basis gate-by-gate to the principal axes of the operator's local polarisation, splitting Pauli complexity into an invariant occupation part and a removable flavour part, and substantially reduces truncation error and memory versus fixed-basis Pauli propagation.
AI.motivation: The cost of Pauli propagation is basis-dependent: depending on the local basis chosen to expand the evolving operator, the number of Pauli strings needed differs. The paper seeks a principled, cheap way to choose local bases that minimise the cost while remaining compatible with the memory structure of Pauli propagation.
AI.method: The authors decompose Pauli complexity into an occupation part (invariant under local rotations, lower-bounded by the operator's mass and length distributions) and a flavour part that a suitable basis can eliminate. They then introduce frame-adaptive Pauli propagation (FAPP), which rotates every qubit's basis gate-by-gate to the principal axes of the operator's local polarisation, performed exactly and within the memory structure of standard Pauli propagation. The local polarisation itself serves as a predictor of the maximum gain achievable by any local frame.
AI.result: In the transverse- and longitudinal-field Ising chain, FAPP lowers truncation error at fixed memory by up to an order of magnitude and reduces memory by a size-independent factor of three. On the infinite two-dimensional lattice it requires up to seven times fewer strings for a given certified accuracy, and in Clifford circuits doped with T gates it needs two to eight times fewer strings.
AI.conclusion: A simple, local, gate-by-gate basis-rotation rule captures most of the benefit of the optimal local frame and reliably predicts attainable gains, yielding substantial reductions in truncation error and memory across diverse models and making FAPP an effective, low-overhead enhancement to Pauli propagation.

title: Model-family selection and recovery-gate design in generator-based noise tomography
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables. Companion paper to arXiv:2611.08310 [quant-ph]
summary: Family selection in generator-model noise tomography, usually quoted as a property of the hardware, is a hypothesis test whose shot floor is closed form, $N^{*}=λ_{\mathrm{req}}/(r_{\mathrm{b}} S)^{2}$, controlled by the absolute bias $r_{\mathrm{b}} S$ rather than by the relative residual $r_{\mathrm{b}}$, and therefore computable for any device before a single shot is taken. The same computation prices the recovery gates, because the fingerprint that fixes a family's residual and the Fisher information that ranks the designs are read off the same map: there is no design-independent verdict and no family-independent design optimum. Whether a design can move that price is structural, not numerical: a bias confined to the block every design measures identically is design-blind, while one that reaches the code blocks can be repriced by a factor of sixty-eight. The two platforms here are its extremes, at $98.1\%$ and $48.0\%$ in the design-blind block. At the reference point the floor is $1.1\times10^{7}$ and $6.7\times10^{6}$ shots per component for the two families, so at the $10^{5}$ shots a run spends the test has power $0.053$ at a level of $0.05$ and the residual it reports is shot noise. Rebuilding the fingerprint under each of the sixty-four designs moves the floor by $68$ on one platform and $1.7$ on the other, and the most precise design costs ten times more shots for the verdict than the cheapest to test. All sixty-four placements are full rank, so the design problem is one of conditioning: at three gates the rms varies by factors of $2.7$ and $3.9$ with placement alone, while the optimum over counts is flat. At five qubits the same rule moves the floor by $21$, while the verdict itself costs $10^{9}$ shots; checked against the calibration of a real three-qubit register, the floor is a requirement on systematic control before it is a shot count.

AI.tldr: Family selection in generator-model noise tomography is reframed as a hypothesis test with a closed-form shot floor N* = λ_req/(r_b S)², controlled by absolute bias r_b S rather than relative residual r_b, and computable for any device before any shots are taken. Design-optimality is shown to be non-universal and structural, with platforms occupying extremes of design-blindness.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to replace the conventional, hardware-attributed view of family selection in noise tomography with a rigorous statistical hypothesis-testing framework that yields a pre-experiment, device-independent cost estimate and clarifies when design choices can actually reduce that cost.
AI.method: The authors derive a closed-form shot floor N* = λ_req/(r_b S)² as a function of absolute bias r_b S; compute the fingerprint (family residual) and Fisher information from the same map to jointly rank designs and price recovery gates; and evaluate sixty-four design placements and gate-count configurations, including a real three-qubit register calibration, to assess rank, conditioning, and design sensitivity.
AI.result: At the reference point, floors are 1.1×10⁷ and 6.7×10⁶ shots per component; at 10⁵ shots the test has power 0.053 at level 0.05, making reported residuals shot noise. Rebuilding fingerprints across sixty-four designs changes the floor by a factor of 68 on one platform and 1.7 on the other; the most precise design costs ten times more shots than the cheapest to test. All sixty-four placements are full rank, reducing the design problem to conditioning: at three gates rms varies by factors of 2.7 and 3.9 with placement alone while the count-optimum is flat; at five qubits the same rule moves the floor by 21 but the verdict costs 10⁹ shots. Platform design-blindness reaches 98.1% and 48.0%.
AI.conclusion: There is no design-independent verdict and no family-independent design optimum. Whether a design can reprice the test is a structural property (design-blind vs. code-block-reachable bias), and in the validated three-qubit setting the floor functions as a requirement on systematic control rather than merely a shot budget.

title: Advantage Distillation in Paired-State Quantum Key Distribution
summary: We investigate advantage distillation for paired-state Loop-Back quantum key distribution, with a fixed optical station serving a lightweight portable terminal. Alice prepares two polarization-encoded pulses, Bob selects and applies a polarization filter to each pulse, and Alice infers his selections from the returned detection pattern. The proposed advantage-distillation step selects consistent blocks of three two-bit records using two independent public parity checks on a minimal connected graph. The closing edge of a parity polygon is shown to be redundant: any spanning tree of the same vertices has the same acceptance set. We derive exact acceptance probabilities, residual-error laws, and retention rates. Under independent bit errors, the three-record filter reduces the leading error term from e to e^2, while its cost in discarded records and public information is accounted for explicitly. A modular security theorem bounds the additional guessing advantage available to an adversary after syndrome disclosure and block acceptance, including arbitrary quantum side information. We also evaluate a specified single-photon passive-tap optical channel, obtaining a positive conditional entropy bound and exact accepted-block security quantities. This parity-based advantage-distillation step detects discrepancies by postselection; it does not correct individual errors and is intended to precede conventional reconciliation. The architecture suggests two further directions: hybrid filtering and reconciliation, and key establishment between portable users accessing a shared quantum station.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes a three-record, parity-check-based advantage distillation step for paired-state Loop-Back QKD between a fixed optical station and a portable terminal, deriving exact acceptance probabilities, error laws, retention rates, and a modular security theorem, and evaluating a passive-tap channel.
AI.motivation: Loop-Back QKD with a lightweight portable terminal and a shared fixed optical station needs robust postselection to suppress errors before conventional reconciliation; the work aims to quantify such a filter's error suppression and its security cost.
AI.method: Alice prepares two polarization-encoded pulses; Bob applies a polarization filter and Alice infers his selections from the returned detection pattern. The distillation step accepts consistent blocks of three two-bit records using two independent public parity checks on a minimal connected graph, showing the closing edge of a parity polygon is redundant (spanning trees yield identical acceptance sets). Exact acceptance probabilities, residual-error laws, and retention rates are derived, a modular security theorem bounds adversarial guessing advantage after syndrome disclosure with arbitrary quantum side information, and a specified single-photon passive-tap channel is evaluated.
AI.result: Under independent bit errors the filter reduces the leading error term from e to e^2, with discarded-record and public-information costs explicitly accounted for. For the passive-tap channel, a positive conditional entropy bound and exact accepted-block security quantities are obtained.
AI.conclusion: The parity-based distillation step performs discrepancy detection via postselection rather than individual error correction and is intended to precede conventional reconciliation. The architecture suggests hybrid filtering-with-reconciliation and key establishment among portable users sharing a quantum station as future directions.

title: An optimal quantum strategy for the $2$-hat game
summary: We study the two-player hat game as a two-input, three-output non-local game. We calculate the quantum commuting value and show that it coincides with the quantum one. In particular, we show that \[ω_{\rm q}(H_2)=ω_{\mathrm{qc}}(H_2)=\frac{15+\sqrt{33}}{36}\approx 0.576238.\] We achieve the optimal quantum advantage using a shared non-maximally entangled qutrit state. To establish optimality, we exploit the game's symmetry under the dihedral group $D_8$ and apply its representation theory to substantially reduce the complexity of the underlying matrix problem. We also determine the no-signalling value $ω_{\mathrm{ns}}(H_2)=2/3$.

AI.tldr: The two-player hat game is analyzed as a two-input, three-output non-local game: its quantum and quantum-commuting values coincide at (15+√33)/36 ≈ 0.576238, while the no-signalling value is 2/3.
AI.motivation: Hat games are natural testbeds for non-local correlations, but their exact quantum values are often unknown. The authors aim to pin down the precise value of the two-player hat game and determine whether the quantum and commuting-operator models coincide for this game.
AI.method: The game is formulated as a two-input, three-output non-local game. The optimal quantum strategy uses a shared non-maximally entangled qutrit state. Optimality is proven by exploiting the game's symmetry under the dihedral group D_8 and applying its representation theory to reduce the dimensionality of the underlying matrix optimization problem. The no-signalling value is computed separately.
AI.result: The quantum value and the quantum commuting value coincide: ω_q(H_2) = ω_qc(H_2) = (15+√33)/36 ≈ 0.576238. The optimal advantage is attained with a non-maximally entangled qutrit. The no-signalling value is ω_ns(H_2) = 2/3.
AI.conclusion: The two-player hat game has equal quantum and quantum-commuting values, so it does not separate these two models, and it exhibits a strictly smaller no-signalling value (2/3), confirming a quantum-versus-no-signalling gap. The D_8 symmetry plus representation theory provides an efficient route to exact optimality proofs.

title: Super-resolution quantum imaging via multiphoton correlation
comment: 6 pages, 5 figurs. Submitted for publication and comments are welcome
summary: The resolution of conventional imaging is fundamentally constrained by the diffraction limit. Here we demonstrate that this limit can be overcome using classical thermal light, through the correlation of multiphoton subsystems. By resolving the photon numbers detected in the two arms of a Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometer, the correlation function exhibits a narrowed peak or dip whose width is tunable via the average photon number. Temporal and spatial super-resolution enhancements up to 11.8-fold and 5.1-fold, respectively, are experimentally achieved. As a proof-of-principle experiment, a double-pinhole that is completely unresolved by standard ghost imaging becomes clearly distinguishable via the correlation of two-photon versus zero-photon. The principle of this super-resolution imaging can be interpreted as a combination of classical super-resolution imaging and quantum super-resolution imaging. This work provides a versatile platform for super-resolution imaging and lithography, and opens a new avenue for exploring the boundary between classical and nonclassical phenomena.

AI.tldr: Classical thermal light beats the diffraction limit via multiphoton-number correlations in a Hanbury Brown–Twiss setup, yielding tunable super-resolution peaks/dips and up to 11.8× (temporal) and 5.1× (spatial) enhancement.
AI.motivation: Conventional imaging is fundamentally constrained by the diffraction limit, and existing super-resolution approaches typically demand nonclassical light or complex setups. The authors aim to show that diffraction-limited resolution can be surpassed using only classical thermal light by exploiting higher-order intensity correlations.
AI.method: Two-arm Hanbury Brown–Twiss interferometry with classical thermal light, in which the photon numbers detected in both arms are resolved and correlated. The resulting correlation function develops a narrowed peak (or dip) whose width is tunable through the average photon number; two-photon versus zero-photon coincidence correlations are used for imaging, tested on a double-pinhole target unresolvable by standard ghost imaging.
AI.result: Temporal super-resolution enhancement of up to 11.8-fold and spatial enhancement of up to 5.1-fold were experimentally achieved. A double-pinhole completely unresolved in standard ghost imaging became clearly distinguishable via two-photon-versus-zero-photon correlation.
AI.conclusion: Super-resolution can be realized with classical thermal light through multiphoton-number correlation, interpreted as a combination of classical and quantum super-resolution imaging. The scheme offers a versatile platform for super-resolution imaging and lithography and probes the boundary between classical and nonclassical phenomena.

title: Long-distance quantum secure direct communication with Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill qubits
summary: The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code possesses a lattice periodic structure that enables the effective correction of small displacement errors induced by noise in phase space, which is indispensable for quantum computation. The GKP code was also used to construct a long-distance entanglement channel in quantum repeaters and distribute random keys in quantum key distribution (QKD). Using GKP encoding, we propose a quantum secure direct communication (QSDC) protocol that not only transmits the secret message directly, but also helps protect the safety of communication personnel. The exponential attenuation loss of photons can be overcome by the third-generation quantum repeater. Numerical simulation results demonstrate that secure transmission distance exceeding 1000 km is achievable with a 23 dB squeezing level. Furthermore, we establish a cost-based optimization framework to characterize the trade-off among secure communication distance, secrecy capacity, and repeater resources, enabling optimized repeater deployment and providing a systematic design strategy for scalable quantum repeater architectures. The results demonstrate the potential of combining GKP error correction for long-distance QSDC and quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a GKP-encoded quantum secure direct communication (QSDC) protocol over third-generation quantum repeaters, achieving >1000 km secure transmission at 23 dB squeezing, and introduces a cost-based framework to optimize the trade-off among distance, secrecy capacity, and repeater resources.
AI.motivation: Photon exponential attenuation limits long-distance quantum communication, and existing GKP applications (entanglement channels, QKD) do not directly transmit secret messages. The authors aim to combine GKP error correction with quantum repeaters to enable long-distance QSDC that also protects communication personnel.
AI.method: GKP encoding is exploited for its lattice periodic structure to correct small phase-space displacement errors, integrated with a third-generation quantum repeater to overcome photon loss. A cost-based optimization framework is established to characterize the trade-off among secure communication distance, secrecy capacity, and repeater resources. Numerical simulation validates performance.
AI.result: Numerical simulations show secure transmission distances exceeding 1000 km at a 23 dB squeezing level. The optimization framework enables optimized repeater deployment and provides a systematic design strategy for scalable quantum repeater architectures.
AI.conclusion: Combining GKP error correction with quantum repeaters is promising for long-distance QSDC and scalable quantum networks, offering a systematic design strategy for repeater deployment.

title: Rotational Encoding of Objective Functions for Quantum Optimization
summary: In this paper, we introduce the Angular Rotational Counter (ARC), a novel approach to represent objective functions that can be decomposed as a weighted sum of Boolean functions. ARC encodes the objective as an accumulated sum of quantum rotations onto a single-qubit register instead of a multi-qubit register used in much of the previous literature. We mathematically establish and experimentally validate that these rotations sum to the objective value for all possible solutions and derive the relationship between the resulting measurement probabilities and the objective. This design was applied to construct a quantum oracle for the state assignment problem of finite automata and state machines using a weighted Hamming distance cost function, which is a special case of the quadratic assignment problem. We evaluate this oracle design on 26 benchmarks and compare it with corresponding Boolean-based oracles on four cost metrics. Across these benchmarks, the oracle with ARC produces a mean reduction in the qubit count of 20.8%, gate count of 89.3%, circuit depth of 92.4%, and quantum cost of 90.6%. These results demonstrate substantial reductions in circuit cost for the evaluated benchmarks and establish rotational encoding as a promising approach for representing objective functions in optimization based on quantum search algorithms.

AI.tldr: A novel Angular Rotational Counter (ARC) is proposed to encode objective functions—decomposable as weighted sums of Boolean functions—as accumulated single-qubit rotations, drastically reducing quantum oracle circuit costs for optimization via quantum search.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches represent objective functions using multi-qubit registers, which is expensive in qubit, gate, and depth resources. A more efficient encoding is needed for objective functions in quantum search-based optimization.
AI.method: ARC encodes the objective as an accumulated sum of quantum rotations onto a single-qubit register instead of a multi-qubit register. The authors mathematically prove and experimentally validate that these rotations sum to the objective value for all solutions, deriving the relation between measurement probabilities and the objective. They apply this to build a quantum oracle for the state assignment problem of finite automata/state machines using a weighted Hamming distance cost (a special case of QAP), benchmarked on 26 instances against Boolean-based oracles on four cost metrics.
AI.result: Relative to Boolean-based oracles, ARC yields mean reductions of 20.8% in qubit count, 89.3% in gate count, 92.4% in circuit depth, and 90.6% in quantum cost across the 26 benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: ARC achieves substantial circuit-cost reductions and establishes rotational encoding as a promising approach for representing objective functions in quantum-search-based optimization.

title: AI-Driven Discovery of Entanglement Witness in Spin Hamiltonians
summary: Entanglement is a crucial resource in quantum science and engineering, but detecting it in many-body states from experimentally accessible observables remains challenging. Here we introduce EntNet, an AI-driven framework to discover compact combinations of spin observables that accurately distinguish entangled from fully separable many-body mixed states in one-dimensional spin-$1/2$ chains governed by short-range Hamiltonians. We construct local-unitary-invariant representations of measurable Pauli correlators up to four-body order, sparsely select 16 candidate invariant feature channels, and learn their spatial structure using a Transformer architecture with rotary positional embeddings. Using only expectation values of these low-order observables, EntNet achieves $>98\%$ recall on certified entangled states with near-zero false-positive rates on separable states. Remarkably, it exhibits transferability across system sizes and distinct Hamiltonian families, including frustrated and disordered spin models, with minimal loss of accuracy. Beyond detection, EntNet provides physical insight into entanglement detection by revealing a selective spatial organization of pair correlations, while its finite-temperature decision boundary tracks the excitation gap of Jordan-Wigner quasiparticles. These results establish a transferable and physically interpretable framework for data-driven discovery of entanglement witnesses from local correlation functions.

AI.tldr: EntNet is an AI framework that learns compact combinations of low-order spin observables to detect entanglement in many-body mixed states with >98% recall, transferring across system sizes and Hamiltonians.
AI.motivation: Detecting entanglement in many-body states from experimentally accessible observables is difficult; the authors aim to find compact, measurable combinations of local correlators that can serve as reliable entanglement witnesses without full state tomography.
AI.method: Construct local-unitary-invariant representations of Pauli correlators up to four-body order; sparsely select 16 candidate invariant feature channels; learn their spatial structure with a Transformer using rotary positional embeddings; train to distinguish entangled from fully separable mixed states in 1D spin-1/2 chains with short-range Hamiltonians.
AI.result: Using only expectation values of low-order observables, EntNet achieves >98% recall on certified entangled states with near-zero false positives on separable states, and transfers across system sizes and Hamiltonian families (including frustrated and disordered models) with minimal accuracy loss. It reveals selective spatial organization of pair correlations and a finite-temperature decision boundary tracking the Jordan-Wigner quasiparticle excitation gap.
AI.conclusion: EntNet offers a transferable, physically interpretable framework for data-driven discovery of entanglement witnesses from local correlation functions, linking learned decision boundaries to underlying quasiparticle physics.

title: Parameterized equivalence checking of quantum circuit generators via weighted automata
comment: main text pp. 1-48, Online Resource 1 pp. 49-64; code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24059428
summary: A generator builds a quantum circuit from the number of qubits and a bit string. We check a generator against a reference for all parameter values under six equivalence relations. For ladder programs, we prove that above a computable threshold the circuit matrices form a uniform matrix product operator, a weighted automaton of dimension independent of the number of qubits. Equivalence reduces to the zeroness of a difference automaton, checked modulo primes. The answer is a counterexample or "equal", exact or with a computed error bound. Experimentally, the method found errors missed by fixed-size checks and produced no incorrect verdicts.

AI.tldr: The paper verifies quantum-circuit generators against a reference across all parameter values under six equivalence relations, proving that "ladder" programs yield uniform matrix product operators whose equivalence reduces to zeroness of a finite difference automaton, checked modulo primes.
AI.motivation: Fixed-size checks miss errors because generators are parameterized by qubit count and bit strings; a sound method is needed to decide equivalence of circuit matrices for all parameter values, not just sampled sizes.
AI.method: For ladder programs, prove that above a computable threshold the circuit matrices form a uniform matrix product operator — a weighted automaton of dimension independent of qubit count. Then reduce equivalence (six relations) to zeroness of a difference automaton, tested modulo primes; output either a counterexample or "equal," exact or with a computed error bound.
AI.result: Experiments found errors missed by fixed-size checks while producing no incorrect verdicts.
AI.conclusion: Uniform matrix product operators plus modular zeroness give a sound, threshold-based decision procedure for quantum-circuit generator equivalence, yielding counterexamples or certified equality.

title: A Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Architecture with Globally Driven Atom Arrays
summary: Scalable quantum computation requires reconciling programmability with simple, high-fidelity control. Here, we propose a universal fault-tolerant architecture using globally driven dual-species atom arrays. In a hybrid neutral-atom system, interspecies Rydberg interactions enable qubit addressability without locally addressed quantum gates. We construct a universal native instruction set, Global Rydberg Atom Instruction Language (GRAIL), and show that crosstalk errors can be suppressed to the $10^{-4}$ level. We compile surface-code error correction and magic state cultivation into GRAIL, and parallelize the compilation to suppress crosstalk. Under a hardware-inferred circuit-level noise model, we obtain an error-correction threshold of $1.43\%$ for the resulting quantum memory and a logical error rate below $10^{-9}$ for magic states cultivated at an experimentally accessible Rydberg Rabi frequency. By replacing local gate addressing with atom-mediated selectivity, this architecture removes the associated calibration requirements, offering a route to simpler control for large-scale fault-tolerant neutral-atom computation.

AI.tldr: A universal fault-tolerant architecture using globally driven dual-species neutral-atom arrays, where interspecies Rydberg interactions provide addressability without local gate addressing, yielding a compiled instruction set (GRAIL) with crosstalk below ~10⁻⁴, a 1.43% surface-code threshold, and magic-state logical error rates below 10⁻⁹.
AI.motivation: Scalable quantum computation requires reconciling programmability with simple, high-fidelity control. Locally addressed quantum gates impose heavy calibration burdens on large neutral-atom systems, motivating an architecture that achieves qubit selectivity through atom-mediated interactions rather than local addressing.
AI.method: Proposes a hybrid dual-species neutral-atom system in which interspecies Rydberg interactions enable qubit addressability under global driving. Builds a universal native instruction set, the Global Rydberg Atom Instruction Language (GRAIL), and compiles surface-code error correction and magic state cultivation into it, parallelizing compilation to suppress crosstalk. Performance is evaluated under a hardware-inferred circuit-level noise model.
AI.result: Crosstalk errors are suppressed to the 10⁻⁴ level. The compiled surface code yields an error-correction threshold of 1.43% for the resulting quantum memory, and magic states cultivated at an experimentally accessible Rydberg Rabi frequency achieve logical error rates below 10⁻⁹.
AI.conclusion: Replacing local gate addressing with atom-mediated selectivity eliminates associated calibration requirements, offering a route to simpler control for large-scale fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum computation.

title: Modular and Looping Quantum Photonic Processing Unit for Quantum Computing
summary: Photonic processors are emerging as promising platforms in the race towards the realization of practical universal quantum computers. Several architectures with universal capabilities have been proposed for their implementation via a photonic platform, each with their own set of benefits and drawbacks. In this work we propose an architecture for a universal photonic quantum computer. The proposed architecture is modular, allowing for a high degree of flexibility and scalability, and relies on a loop-based structure, significantly reducing the number of physical components required to implement it experimentally. We prove that our architecture is universal, deterministic, and compatible with the quantum circuital model, as well as reprogrammable and capable of adaptive measurements. Furthermore, we showcase its functioning via numerical simulation on specific examples, by using machine learning techniques on a set of fundamental linear and nonlinear optical components to obtain some of the building blocks used in the architecture. The obtained results can be used to highlight the benefits and the drawbacks of the proposed architecture, as well as the route for future developments towards its physical implementation.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a modular, loop-based architecture for a universal photonic quantum computer that is universal, deterministic, circuit-model compatible, reprogrammable, and supports adaptive measurements, while reducing the physical component count; they validate it via numerical simulation using machine learning to realize optical building blocks.
AI.motivation: Practical universal quantum computing remains unrealized, and photonic platforms are promising candidates. Existing universal photonic architectures each carry distinct benefits and drawbacks, motivating a design that improves scalability, flexibility, and experimental feasibility.
AI.method: An architecture for a universal photonic quantum computer built on a loop-based, modular structure. The authors provide proofs of universality, determinism, compatibility with the quantum circuit model, reprogrammability, and adaptive measurement capability. They demonstrate functioning through numerical simulation on specific examples, applying machine learning techniques to a set of fundamental linear and nonlinear optical components to obtain architecture building blocks.
AI.result: The architecture is shown to be universal, deterministic, circuit-model compatible, reprogrammable, and capable of adaptive measurements, with a significantly reduced number of physical components due to the loop-based design. Numerical simulations on specific examples, supported by ML-derived optical building blocks, illustrate its operation and expose both advantages and limitations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed loop-based modular architecture offers a flexible, scalable, and experimentally economical route toward universal photonic quantum computing. The simulation results clarify its benefits and drawbacks and outline directions for future development toward physical implementation.

authors: Jean-Louis de Bougrenet de la Tocnaye
title: High Rate Quantum Block Turbo Codes
summary: Quantum Block Turbo Code is an iterative decoding technique for concatenated quantum error correction codes in product form. In this paper, we study new high rate quantum block turbo codes with different constituent codes. We examine the impact of the change of codes parameters and the order of constituent codes on turbo performance.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates new high-rate quantum block turbo codes (QBTCs) built from different constituent codes and analyzes how code parameters and the ordering of constituent codes affect turbo decoding performance.
AI.motivation: Quantum block turbo codes offer iterative decoding for concatenated quantum error correction codes in product form, but the design space of constituent codes and their arrangement remains insufficiently explored, particularly for high-rate regimes.
AI.method: Design of high-rate QBTCs using product-form concatenation with varied constituent codes, followed by evaluation of the effects of changing code parameters and the order/placement of constituent codes on iterative turbo decoding performance.
AI.result: The study characterizes how variations in constituent code parameters and their ordering influence the performance of the resulting high-rate QBTCs.
AI.conclusion: Constituent code selection and ordering are meaningful design levers for high-rate quantum block turbo codes, informing practical construction choices for iterative quantum error correction.

title: Testing non-classical gravitational phase dynamics under strong dephasing
summary: Whether gravity must be quantum is often approached by asking whether two masses can become entangled through their mutual gravitational interaction. In practice, the weak interaction competes with environmental decoherence, so the final state may contain no entanglement even when the underlying gravitational phase remains coherent. We investigate what can still be learned from the dynamics in a dephased Bose--Marletto--Vedral setup. The dominant Newtonian effect for well-separated paths is an accumulated phase rather than transfer between interferometer arms, a regime motivated by matter-wave gravitational phase experiments and quantified here by wavepacket-overlap and deflection estimates. Keeping independently characterized local which-path dephasing fixed, we prove an exact finite-time distinction between the gravitational conditional-phase evolution and every passive stochastic local-phase model (induced by a classical mediator), including regimes where the chosen input remains separable at all times. The distinction survives, with a modified sensitivity, when the comparison is enlarged to population-preserving classical measurement and feedback through a diagonal PPT relaxation. These results identify an operational test of gravitational phase dynamics in the strong-dephasing regimes, conditional on explicit and physically motivated classical mediator models.

AI.tldr: Even under strong local which-path dephasing, gravitational conditional-phase dynamics can be distinguished exactly (in finite time) from every passive stochastic classical-mediator model, including regimes where the state stays separable throughout.
AI.motivation: Entanglement-based tests of whether gravity is quantum are hampered because weak gravitational interaction competes with environmental decoherence, so final states may show no entanglement even if the gravitational phase stays coherent. The authors ask what gravitational signatures survive in this dephased regime.
AI.method: Analyze a dephased Bose–Marletto–Vedral setup in the regime where the dominant Newtonian effect is an accumulated conditional phase rather than arm-to-arm population transfer (justified via wavepacket-overlap and deflection estimates). With independently characterized local which-path dephasing held fixed, they prove an exact finite-time distinction between the gravitational conditional-phase evolution and all passive stochastic local-phase models induced by a classical mediator. They extend the comparison to population-preserving classical measurement and feedback using a diagonal PPT relaxation.
AI.result: An exact finite-time operational distinction between gravitational phase dynamics and classical-mediator models holds even where the input state remains separable at all times; the distinction persists with modified sensitivity when enlarged to population-preserving classical measurement/feedback.
AI.conclusion: Provides an operational test of gravitational phase dynamics in strong-dephasing regimes, conditional on explicit, physically motivated classical-mediator models rather than on entanglement generation.

title: Commuting-check gauging for fault-tolerant logical measurements
summary: Gauging turns a logical operator into a product of local checks, providing a route to logical measurement and lattice surgery. These checks can fail to commute outside the code space, so measuring one can randomize the outcome of another. In this work, we introduce completion qubits that make the checks commute for Clifford $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetries of qubit stabilizer codes. Adding one completion qubit per noncommuting pair preserves the gauged code space and its distance while keeping the checks Clifford. Completion also preserves the low-density parity-check property with a constant-factor qubit overhead. We generalize completion to qudits and establish bounds on the Clifford-hierarchy level of the completed checks in prime dimensions. Global commutation ensures that a fault-free round fixes the syndrome until the next fault and allows us to bound fault propagation independently of the number of measurement rounds. For qubit codes, we show that gauging and ungauging a distance-$d$ parent code implements a logical measurement with circuit fault distance $Ω(d)$ in $O(d)$ rounds. We demonstrate the construction by gauging two toric codes into the $D(D_4)$ quantum double and back, with an explicit circuit whose circuit fault distance equals the parent code distance. Our results provide a framework for fault-tolerant logical measurements using commuting checks, with applications to magic-state preparation by lattice surgery.

AI.tldr: Introducing "completion qubits" to make gauged checks commute within the code space for Clifford Z2 symmetries of qubit stabilizer codes, enabling fault-tolerant logical measurements with commuting checks, bounded fault propagation, and Ω(d) circuit fault distance.
AI.motivation: Gauging converts a logical operator into a product of local checks, offering a path to logical measurement and lattice surgery. However, these checks need not commute outside the code space, so measuring one check can randomize the outcome of another, undermining reliable syndrome extraction and fault tolerance.
AI.method: The authors add one completion qubit per noncommuting check pair to enforce commutation for Clifford Z2 symmetries of qubit stabilizer codes, preserving the gauged code space, distance, and Clifford nature of checks. The construction is generalized to qudits, with bounds established on the Clifford-hierarchy level of completed checks in prime dimensions. Fault analysis bounds fault propagation in a fault-free round independently of the number of measurement rounds, and gauging/ungauging a distance-d parent code is used to implement logical measurement. The construction is demonstrated by gauging two toric codes into the D(D4) quantum double and back.
AI.result: Completion preserves the gauged code space and distance, keeps checks Clifford, and retains the low-density parity-check property with constant-factor qubit overhead. Global commutation ensures a fault-free round fixes the syndrome until the next fault, bounding fault propagation independent of measurement rounds. For qubit codes, gauging and ungauging a distance-d parent code yields a logical measurement with circuit fault distance Ω(d) in O(d) rounds; the toric-to-D(D4) example gives an explicit circuit whose circuit fault distance equals the parent code distance.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables fault-tolerant logical measurements using commuting checks, with applications to magic-state preparation via lattice surgery.

title: Deploying QKD on the fiber links of the National Quantum Communication Infrastructure in Sweden
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is being deployed across Europe to evaluate its performance and practicality in real-world scenarios. When preparing this deployment, it is important to survey the properties of the fiber links that will be used for the quantum channel, cross-checking them with those of QKD devices, to ensure compatibility and optimal performance. We report here our studies from the Swedish chapter of this endeavor, the National Quantum Communication Infrastructure in Sweden. We focus on procedures to characterize the links and evaluate their suitability for QKD. We relate measurable properties to the key factors that affect the secret key rate using a simplified model that aims at the essence of QKD performance. Finally, we confirm the feasibility of QKD on one of our links by reporting a one-month long successful test.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys and characterizes deployed fiber links in Sweden's national quantum communication infrastructure, linking measurable link properties to QKD secret key rate via a simplified performance model, and confirms feasibility with a one-month QKD test.
AI.motivation: As QKD is being deployed across Europe, deployments must verify that the fiber links intended for the quantum channel are compatible with the QKD devices, ensuring optimal real-world performance. This requires systematic characterization of link properties.
AI.method: The authors define procedures to characterize fiber links and assess their QKD suitability, and map measurable link properties onto the key factors governing secret key rate using a simplified model capturing the essence of QKD performance.
AI.result: They evaluate the suitability of the studied links and demonstrate the feasibility of QKD on one link through a successful one-month long test.
AI.conclusion: QKD is feasible on the characterized deployed fiber links, and the proposed characterization procedures and simplified model provide a practical basis for cross-checking links against QKD device requirements.

title: Calibration-free quantum thermometry with strain-swept two-level defects
comment: Main: 9 pages, 6 figures; Supplemental Material: 17 pages, 5 figures
summary: Superconducting qubits operate within a well-defined temperature range, making local temperature monitoring important. Here we show that intrinsic two-level defects in Josephson-junction barriers can act as local thermometers by exploiting the shape of their population response, without requiring calibration of the readout offset or contrast. Marginalizing over these unknown parameters imposes an identifiability requirement absent from single-parameter thermometric bounds: for narrow sweeps, usable information scales as the fourth power of the sweep width. Hence, a narrow sweep becomes locally indistinguishable from a change in offset or contrast. We illustrate this principle with a strain-swept two-level defect in a Josephson junction. For a reported defect with tunneling energy $Δ_{0}/h=\SI{1.3}{\giga\hertz}$, swept along one branch of its hyperbola to \SI{2.69}{\giga\hertz} (an asymmetry excursion of \SI{2.36}{\giga\hertz}, or \SI{8}{\volt} of piezo voltage), the analysis projects a single-defect fit precision of \SI{0.58}{\percent} at \SI{20}{\milli\kelvin}. The resulting response enables temperature estimation without prior calibration of the readout offset and contrast, while the same sweep overdetermines the Boltzmann form and identifies significant deviations from thermality. These results establish intrinsic junction defects as a resource for calibration-free local thermometry and highlight identifiability as a key design criterion for primary temperature sensing.

AI.tldr: Intrinsic two-level defects in Josephson-junction barriers can serve as calibration-free local thermometers by exploiting the shape of their population response, provided the sweep is wide enough to keep temperature identifiable relative to unknown readout offset and contrast.
AI.motivation: Superconducting qubits operate in a narrow temperature range, so local temperature monitoring matters, yet conventional readout requires calibrating offset and contrast. The authors seek a primary (calibration-free) thermometry scheme and identify a subtle obstacle: marginalizing over unknown readout parameters adds an identifiability constraint that single-parameter thermometric bounds ignore.
AI.method: Treat intrinsic two-level defects in Josephson-junction barriers as local thermometers whose population response versus a swept parameter (via strain/piezo tuning of a hyperbola branch) encodes temperature. Analytically derive the identifiability requirement after marginalizing over offset and contrast, and apply the framework to a reported defect with tunneling energy Δ0/h = 1.3 GHz, swept to 2.69 GHz (2.36 GHz asymmetry excursion, 8 V piezo).
AI.result: For narrow sweeps, usable information scales as the fourth power of sweep width, so a narrow sweep is locally indistinguishable from an offset or contrast change. For the cited defect at 20 mK, the projected single-defect fit precision is 0.58%. The same sweep overdetermines the Boltzmann form and reveals significant deviations from thermality.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic junction defects constitute a resource for calibration-free local thermometry, and identifiability—not merely sensitivity—should be a key design criterion for primary temperature sensing in superconducting qubit platforms.

title: Attainable and unattainable quantum precision limits in ultrastrong light--matter coupling
summary: In this paper, we study the gauge dependence of quantum precision in ultrastrongly coupled light--matter systems. The unitary between gauges carries the coupling $g$, so each truncation defines a different family. The quantum Fisher information traces an exact parabola across frames. Harmonic matter minimizes it at a universal $θ_\ast=Ω/(Ω+ω)$, set by the matter and cavity frequencies. Only the minimal-coupling bound is attainable. Frames differ by a factor $9.6$ with opposite trends. Diverging virtual-excitation gain at the Dicke point is a gauge artifact and saturates.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how the choice of gauge affects quantum precision (quantum Fisher information) in ultrastrongly coupled light–matter systems, showing that gauge choice introduces a frame-dependent coupling, produces an exact parabolic trajectory of QFI, and that apparent divergences at the Dicke point are gauge artifacts.
AI.motivation: In ultrastrong coupling, the unitary transforming between gauges (minimal-coupling vs. dipole) carries the coupling strength g, so truncation schemes define different, frame-dependent families of models. This raises the question of how robust quantum precision estimates are under gauge choice, and whether reported divergences in virtual-excitation gain are physical or artifacts.
AI.method: The authors compute the quantum Fisher information across gauges and show it traces an exact parabola as a function of the frame parameter. They consider harmonic matter and derive the gauge parameter minimizing QFI, then compare attainable precision bounds across frames.
AI.result: QFI follows an exact parabola across frames, with harmonic matter minimizing it at a universal value θ* = Ω/(Ω+ω) determined by matter frequency Ω and cavity frequency ω. Only the minimal-coupling bound is attainable; frames differ by a factor of 9.6 with opposite trends. The divergence of virtual-excitation gain at the Dicke point is a gauge artifact and saturates.
AI.conclusion: Gauge choice strongly affects precision estimates in ultrastrongly coupled systems, but the minimal-coupling bound is the only physically attainable one. Apparent divergences at the Dicke point are artifacts that saturate, underscoring the need for gauge-covariant treatment of quantum metrology in this regime.

title: Universal two-qubit control across dilution refrigerators via a 10-km coherent optical link
summary: Distributed quantum networks are important for scalable quantum processors and for potential applications in communication, distributed computation, and sensing, in which direct classical links for adaptive control are essential to harness the shared entanglement. However, controlling superconducting quantum processors from a separate refrigerator over long distances remains elusive. Here, we introduce a coherent optical link (COL) that delivers microwave waveforms and their phase references between dilution refrigerators. Combining a laser, a microwave-to-optical transducer and an optical-to-microwave photodiode, the COL transmits microwave control signals over 10~km of fiber, while optical references derived from the same laser compensate for the frequency mismatch between devices. Through the COL, we deliver a universal gate set to a transmon qubit and a cavity qubit in another refrigerator and entangle them, and achieve a Bell-state fidelity of 80.6\%. Quantum control delivered through the COL thus provides a classical backbone for modular quantum processors.

AI.tldr: A coherent optical link (COL) transmits microwave control waveforms and phase references between dilution refrigerators over 10 km of fiber, enabling remote quantum control and entanglement of qubits in separate fridges with 80.6% Bell-state fidelity.
AI.motivation: Distributed quantum networks require direct classical links for adaptive control to exploit shared entanglement, but controlling superconducting processors from a separate refrigerator over long distances has remained elusive.
AI.method: The COL combines a laser, a microwave-to-optical transducer, and an optical-to-microwave photodiode to deliver microwave waveforms over 10 km of fiber, while optical references from the same laser compensate for frequency mismatch between devices. Using the link, a universal gate set is delivered to a transmon qubit and a cavity qubit located in another refrigerator, which are then entangled.
AI.result: Remote entanglement of the two qubits is achieved with a Bell-state fidelity of 80.6%.
AI.conclusion: Quantum control delivered through the COL provides a classical backbone for modular/distributed superconducting quantum processors.

title: An Alternative to Quantum Theory
summary: Despite the remarkable empirical success of quantum theory, the interpretation of measurement and the nature of entanglement correlations remain open questions. We outline an alternative framework that seeks to recover the empirical results of quantum theory from a holistic, scale-invariant ontology. Assuming only point particles in Euclidean space, characterised by ratios of masses (and charges) and by the ratios of their mutual separations, the theory describes shapes through a single scale-invariant function; no dynamical evolution is required. In principle, this framework provides a unified description of finite subsystems embedded in a configuration of infinitely many particles and offers a possible route to deriving the observed structures of atoms, molecules and macroscopic bodies without invoking standard quantum mechanics.

AI.tldr: The paper sketches a scale-invariant, purely geometric framework of point particles whose shapes are encoded in a single scale-invariant function, aiming to reproduce quantum empirical results without dynamical evolution or standard quantum mechanics.
AI.motivation: The empirical success of quantum theory is remarkable, yet the interpretation of measurement and the nature of entanglement correlations remain unresolved, motivating an alternative ontology.
AI.method: Assume only point particles in Euclidean space, characterised by mass (and charge) ratios and ratios of mutual separations; describe configurations via a single scale-invariant shape function, with no dynamical evolution required.
AI.result: The framework is claimed, in principle, to unify the description of finite subsystems embedded within an infinite-particle configuration and to offer a route to deriving structures of atoms, molecules and macroscopic bodies.
AI.conclusion: A holistic, scale-invariant geometric ontology may recover quantum empirical results and derive observed physical structures without invoking standard quantum mechanics.

title: Singularising quantum channels preserving kappa-additivity
summary:
We construct quantum channels by averaging unitary shift conjugations with respect to $κ$-additive probability measures on measurable abelian groups.
  The channels act on the duals of operator algebras generated by shifts and bounded measurable multiplication operators.
  They preserve $κ$-additivity of quantum states and admit a weak-$*$ integral representation on this class.
  If the averaging measure vanishes on singletons, every output state is singular.
  In the appendix, we also establish the corresponding Fubini's theorem for $κ$-additive measures.

AI.tldr: Quantum channels are built by averaging unitary shift conjugations over $\kappa$-additive measures on measurable abelian groups; they preserve $\kappa$-additivity of states, admit a weak-$*$ integral representation, and produce singular outputs whenever the averaging measure vanishes on singletons.
AI.motivation: Shift-based averaging constructions are a standard source of quantum channels, but the existing framework is largely restricted to countably additive (or finitely additive) measures. Extending to $\kappa$-additive measures on measurable abelian groups is needed to handle states and algebras arising in non-separable or large-cardinal settings, where countable additivity is insufficient and the usual integral machinery (including Fubini) is unavailable.
AI.method: For a measurable abelian group and a $\kappa$-additive probability measure on it, define a channel as the average of conjugations by unitary shift operators, acting on the duals of operator algebras generated by shifts together with bounded measurable multiplication operators. Establish preservation of $\kappa$-additivity of quantum states and derive a weak-$*$ integral representation valid on this class of states. Prove singularity of every output state under the hypothesis that the averaging measure vanishes on singletons. Supply, in an appendix, a Fubini-type theorem for $\kappa$-additive measures to justify interchanging the relevant integrals.
AI.result: The constructed maps are genuine quantum channels on the duals of shift-and-multiplication algebras; they preserve $\kappa$-additivity of states and admit a weak-$*$ integral representation over these states. If the averaging measure vanishes on singletons, all output states are singular. A corresponding Fubini theorem for $\kappa$-additive measures is established.
AI.conclusion: Averaging unitary shift conjugations against $\kappa$-additive measures yields a well-behaved class of channels that retain $\kappa$-additivity and possess a weak-$*$ integral representation, with a clean singularity criterion (non-atomicity of the averaging measure) and the necessary measure-theoretic tool (a $\kappa$-additive Fubini theorem) developed alongside.

title: All-to-all connectivity via adiabatic ZZ interactions in a superconducting flux qubit processor
summary: Scalable superconducting quantum processors would benefit from high qubit connectivity, yet existing architectures connect neighbouring qubits via tunable couplers, which introduce substantial wiring and control overhead. Here, we propose a baseband-driven adiabatic ZZ gate that entangles any selected pair in a register of flux qubits coupled via a common cavity. The qubits stay dc-biased at their flux sweet spot. Strong drives applied selectively through local flux lines, at frequencies far below the qubit transitions, adiabatically tilt the quantization axes and generate an effective longitudinal ZZ interaction. The strength of the coupling is tunable and controlled by the amplitudes and relative phase of the drives rather than by any resonance condition. Numerical simulations give coherent gate errors below $10^{-4}$ over broad ranges of drive frequency, with comparable fidelities for two simultaneous gates in a four-qubit register. The protocol is robust against frequency fluctuations and remains effective even when many qubits are coupled to the cavity.

AI.tldr: A baseband-driven adiabatic ZZ gate entangles any selected pair of flux qubits coupled to a common cavity, using off-resonant local flux drives at the sweet spot to generate a tunable longitudinal ZZ interaction with simulated errors below 10^-4.
AI.motivation: Conventional superconducting architectures connect only neighbouring qubits via tunable couplers, which incur substantial wiring and control overhead. High qubit connectivity with reduced overhead is desirable for scalable processors.
AI.method: Flux qubits are dc-biased at their flux sweet spot and coupled via a common cavity. Strong local flux-line drives at frequencies far below qubit transitions adiabatically tilt quantization axes, producing an effective longitudinal ZZ interaction whose strength is set by drive amplitudes and relative phase rather than by resonance conditions. Validated by numerical simulation.
AI.result: Simulations yield coherent gate errors below 10^-4 over broad drive-frequency ranges, with comparable fidelities for two simultaneous gates in a four-qubit register. The protocol is robust against frequency fluctuations and remains effective with many qubits coupled to the cavity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed baseband-driven adiabatic ZZ gate offers all-to-all-pair connectivity in a cavity-coupled flux-qubit register, with tunable, resonance-free control, low simulated error, and scalability to larger qubit counts.

title: Long-Range Ergotropy Transfer with Weakened Boundary-Coupling Spin Chains
summary: Ergotropy is a key quantity of a quantum battery that measures the maximum extractable energy. When the extraction process is not local, a faithful transfer of ergotropy across distance is necessary. In this work, we investigate such transfer by using spin chains with weakened coupling at the boundaries as mediator. Weakening the coupling at the two boundaries of the chain gives rise to localized edge states allowing high fidelity transfer within given time duration. We found that, for long spin chains, the transferred ergotropy alternates between even and odd number of spins. We explain this parity effect by investigating the chain spectral structure. Furthermore, we consider both the nearest-neighbor and long-range interactions between spin. In both model of interactions, weakening the boundary couplings improves the maximum transferred ergotropy for long spin chain, compared with in the case of conventional uniform chain. Although the long-range interaction reduces the transferred ergotropy, the transfer time is reduced, too, in particular for longer chain. In addition to the total transferred ergotropy, we also investigate the effect of initial states of the sender spin to the transport of the coherent and incoherent components of the total ergotropy, and the average transport efficiency.

AI.tldr: Weakly-coupled boundary spin chains act as mediators that transfer quantum battery ergotropy with high fidelity; boundary weakening boosts maximum transferred ergotropy in long chains, with a parity effect between even and odd spin numbers, and long-range hopping trades ergotropy for faster transfer.
AI.motivation: Ergotropy quantifies the maximum extractable energy of a quantum battery, but when energy extraction is non-local, ergotropy must be faithfully transferred over distance. The paper seeks a mediator design that preserves ergotropy during transport.
AI.method: Spin chains with weakened coupling at both boundaries are used as the transfer channel, exploiting the resulting localized edge states for high-fidelity transfer within a fixed time. Both nearest-neighbor and long-range inter-spin interactions are modeled. The chain spectral structure is analyzed to explain observed behavior, and the sender spin's initial state is varied to separate coherent and incoherent ergotropy components and to evaluate average transport efficiency.
AI.result: For long chains the transferred ergotropy alternates with even/odd spin number, explained via the spectral structure. In both interaction models, weakened boundary couplings improve the maximum transferred ergotropy relative to a uniform chain for long chains. Long-range interactions lower transferred ergotropy but shorten transfer time, especially for longer chains. Initial-state dependence governs the transport of coherent versus incoherent ergotropy and the average efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Boundary weakening in spin chains is an effective knob for ergotropy transfer in extended quantum batteries, yielding parity-dependent, spectrally explained improvements; long-range interactions offer a speed–fidelity trade-off, and initial-state preparation of the sender affects coherent/incoherent transport efficiency.

title: Reducing Provers in Distributed Quantum Verification
comment: 22 pages (including references), 4 figures. Submitted to SIROCCO 2027
summary:
In the distributed quantum Merlin-Arthur ($\mathsf{dQMA}$) model introduced by Fraigniaud, Le Gall, Nishimura, and Paz (ITCS 2021), a network of quantum computers verifies a global property with the aid of a quantum proof supplied by an untrusted prover. While the nodes are computationally unbounded, the challenge is to limit proof size and the communication required for verification. In this paper, we consider the model of Hasegawa, Kundu, and Nishimura (PODC 2024), where the proof must be unentangled across nodes, and define its extension to $k$ unentangled provers, denoted by $\mathsf{dQMAS}(k)$. In this setting, we investigate the proof size per node and the communication costs of reducing the number of provers.
  Our first result reduces the number of provers from $k$ to two, doubling the proof size without additional communication. Moreover, with four additional rounds, we can reduce the number of provers from $k$ to one, using at most three times the original local proof size plus a logarithmic term in the number of nodes. Finally, we establish amplification for perfectly complete protocols. In this regime, a single prover suffices with a constant-factor overhead in our reductions, yielding $\mathsf{dQMAS} = \mathsf{dQMAS}(k)$.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the distributed quantum Merlin-Arthur model to k unentangled provers (dQMAS(k)) and shows how to reduce the number of provers (to two, or to one) with bounded proof-size and communication overhead, establishing amplification for perfectly complete protocols and the collapse dQMAS = dQMAS(k).
AI.motivation: In the dQMA model, a network of unbounded quantum computers verifies a global property using a quantum proof from an untrusted prover, with the challenge being to limit proof size and verification communication. The work builds on the Hasegawa–Kundu–Nishimura (PODC 2024) model where the proof must be unentangled across nodes, and asks about proof size per node and the communication cost of reducing the number of unentangled provers.
AI.method: Defines dQMAS(k), the extension of the unentangled-proof dQMA model to k unentangled provers. Develops prover-reduction transformations: a reduction from k provers to two that doubles proof size with no extra communication, and a reduction from k provers to one using four additional rounds with at most three times the original local proof size plus a logarithmic term in the number of nodes. Also establishes amplification for perfectly complete protocols.
AI.result: Prover count can be reduced from k to two with only a factor-2 increase in proof size and no additional communication; from k to one with four extra rounds at cost ≤3× local proof size plus O(log n). Amplification for perfectly complete protocols yields a single prover with constant-factor overhead in these reductions.
AI.conclusion: The number of unentangled provers in distributed quantum verification can be compressed without prohibitive overhead; under perfect completeness a single prover suffices up to constant factors, giving dQMAS = dQMAS(k).

title: Effective Time Advance of Quantum Clocks under Postselection
summary: In the familiar twin paradox, the traveling twin ages less than the one who stays behind as a consequence of relativistic time dilation. Here, we show that quantum postselection can effectively reverse this outcome. Using an analytically solvable quantum clock model, we demonstrate that postselection of the center-of-mass motion produces an effective time advance through anomalous weak values, even though every individual motional branch undergoes ordinary time dilation. We extend this analysis to a weak gravitational field and show that an effective time advance can arise even for simple coherent states of the quantum clock motion. We further illustrate this effect using a hydrogen-like atom, revealing how it manifests itself in the atomic wavefunction. Our results demonstrate that quantum interference and postselection can produce an effective time advance beyond conventional relativistic time dilation.

AI.tldr: Quantum postselection can reverse the twin-paradox outcome: postselection of a clock's center-of-mass motion yields an effective time advance via anomalous weak values, even though each motional branch undergoes ordinary time dilation; this persists in weak gravitational fields and is illustrated with a hydrogen-like atom.
AI.motivation: In the standard twin paradox, relativistic time dilation always makes the traveling twin younger. The authors ask whether quantum postselection and interference can effectively reverse this outcome, i.e., produce an effective time advance opposing conventional relativistic time dilation.
AI.method: An analytically solvable quantum clock model: a clock (internal degree of freedom) coupled to center-of-mass motion that undergoes time dilation. Quantum postselection of the center-of-mass motion is applied, and the resulting effective evolution is evaluated through anomalous weak values. The treatment is extended to a weak gravitational field for simple coherent states, and to a hydrogen-like atom whose atomic wavefunction reveals the effect.
AI.result: Postselection of the center-of-mass motion produces an effective time advance driven by anomalous weak values, although every individual motional branch separately exhibits ordinary time dilation. The effective advance also arises in a weak gravitational field for simple coherent states, and manifests itself in the atomic wavefunction of a hydrogen-like atom.
AI.conclusion: Quantum interference combined with postselection can generate an effective time advance beyond conventional relativistic time dilation, showing that quantum-mechanical effects can qualitatively alter relativistic clock behavior in both special and weak-field gravitational settings.

title: Quantum Residual Exploration for Selected Configuration Interaction
comment: 19 pages, 10 figures; includes End Matter and Supplemental Material
summary: We propose a modular hybrid quantum-classical method to improve selected configuration interaction at a fixed final determinant budget. Quantum measurements supply complementary determinants, accepted only when they outrank classical candidates under a common energetic criterion. This targets multistep excitations that perturbative discovery may miss in strongly correlated systems. A demonstration on the Quantinuum Reimei trapped-ion quantum computer shows that measured proposals for H$_{12}$ at a stretched geometry lower the variational energy relative to classical-only selection at the same final determinant budget.

AI.tldr: A modular hybrid quantum-classical scheme injects quantum-measured determinants into selected configuration interaction, admitting them only if they outrank classical candidates at equal final determinant budget; demonstrated on a trapped-ion QPU for stretched H12.
AI.motivation: Classical selected CI with perturbative determinant discovery can miss higher-order (multistep) excitations that dominate strongly correlated, stretched-bond regimes. The authors seek to improve wavefunction quality at a fixed, controlled determinant budget.
AI.method: Modular hybrid quantum-classical loop: quantum measurements generate candidate determinants that are merged with classical candidates and screened by a common energetic criterion, so quantum proposals are accepted only when they outrank classical ones under the same final determinant budget. Implemented on the Quantinuum Reimei trapped-ion quantum computer for H12 at a stretched geometry.
AI.result: Measured quantum proposals lowered the variational energy relative to classical-only selection at the identical final determinant budget, indicating quantum sampling contributes determinants not efficiently surfaced by perturbative discovery.
AI.conclusion: Quantum measurement can complement classical selected CI as an add-on determinant generator, with a fair budget-matched comparison; the approach targets multistep excitations in strongly correlated systems and is hardware-agnostic/modular.

title: No Exponential Quantum Advantage for Decoded Quantum Interferometry with Local Quantum Decoders
summary: Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) reduces optimization of sparse linear constraint problems, and sampling from their Gibbs measures, to decoding a linear code from a quantum state.
